# The Obscure Origins of the Game of Poker

[1 Reply](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/2020/10/12/the-obscure-origins-of-the-game-of-poker/#comments)

Hello,

This morning, for some strange reason, my mind is on the game of _poker_. Not the _poker_ you use to stir up your fire (which dates to the 1530s in English and yes, it does relate to being a object used to _poke_ the fire).

As I’ve found before when looking at words around card playing, there’s little definitive clarity to be found when it comes to _poker_. This seems appropriate to me as a total _poker_ amateur. On the rare nights when our family sits down for a game we all have to refer to the sheet of rules on which hands beat others. I suspect this means we would be easy prey for any hustler in a hundred mile radius. Luckily we play only for the plastic chips, and the bragging rights of being the winner.

[![Image 2](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/poker.jpg?w=1024)](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/poker.jpg)

Sadly this is not the hand I usually get when playing

Bragging is appropriate as it turns out. An earlier version of the game was called _Brag_. I think I recall them playing it in Jane Austen novels?

Even if you’ve never played a hand of _poker_ in earnest I’m sure you’ve seen it played in movies – by cowboys in a saloon, gangsters in a back room, or grifters in a casino. The game first appeared around the late 1820s, perhaps starting amongst riverboat gamblers on the great Mississippi river. As a result the word entered English with thanks to the Americans.

It wasn’t entirely American however. There was an earlier card game called _Pochspiel_ in German. _Spiel_ means play or game, and the _Poch_ part of the word comes from _pochen_(the verb to brag or bluff). There may even have been a French game called _poque_ which was very similar. It appears that several countries had card games involving bluffing around the same time period and any of them could have been the original source but the American gamblers slipped the word into mainstream English usage and usually take credit on this one. Whist, another very popular card game (this time taught to me by a nun in the 1980s!) also involves bluffing and it dates back to the 1660s, so _poker_ isn’t the first by any means.

The related term is, of course, _poker face_. Early examples of its use to describe somebody controlling their facial expressions to improve their chances in the game date back to the 1870s. This is something I’ve yet to achieve so it’s probably best that I stick to playing with plastic chips rather than cash.

Until next time happy reading, writing, and wordfooling,

Grace ([@wordfoolery](link_10))

**Series Description:**

Hamster Stew is a diary-style comedy serial about the adventures of an Irish mom, Trish McTaggart, struggling with her teenage son, a scary ten year old daughter, and an out of control life which lurches from disaster to chaos. All she wants is a part-time job, more passion with her Scottish husband, and a hands-off mother-in-law but life, and her daughter, are conspiring against her dreams.

Perhaps the lessons her friend is giving her in "how to say no" will help?

**Category/Genre(s):** Humor, Journal Entries  
**Updated:** Weekly  
**Status:** Completed 

  
![Image 2](link_6)

  

**Author Bio For [Grace Tierney](https://channillo.com/series/hamster-stew-and-other-stories/):**

Grace Tierney (www.gracetierney.com) is a columnist, author, and blogger writing in rural Ireland who collects stories of parenting disasters.

She’s been blogging about unusual words at http://wordfoolery.wordpress.com [link_9] since 2009 and has published four word history books “How to Get Your Name in the Dictionary”, "Words the Sea Gave Us", "Words the Vikings Gave Us", and "Words Christmas Gave Us". Grace tweets @Wordfoolery.

**Acknowledgements:**

Many thanks, as always, to Brendan, Daniel, and Eleanor. Don't worry, you're nothing like Trish's family.

I'm lucky enough to volunteer as a writing mentor on National Novel Writing Month each November and this series was begun during Camp NaNoWriMo July 2017. If you've ever wanted to write a story - it's a great place to start.

# [Wordfoolery](link_0)

## Fooling with words since 2009

[![Image 1](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/banner-sep-2024.jpeg)](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/ [link_0])

# My Books

Looking for my **Media Kit**? Try [here](link_1).

![Image 2](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/weather-ebook-cover-jpeg.jpg)
Words the Weather Gave Us

**“Words the Weather Gave Us” (2026) is Coming Soon!**

Launching on the 9th of November 2026, the fourth book in the Words series provides all the words you need to chat about the weather, from _afterclap_ to _zephyr_, along with the stories behind them. Ever since early English runes were named for _hail, ice,_ and _sun_ and helped form the language, we’ve been talking about the weather.This book explores delightful words like _petrichor, degombling, apricity, bumbershoot, dreich,_ and _impluvious_ alongside words borrowed by English from all around the world.More than 330 words and phrases are featured – drawn from clouds, weather folklore and phrases, storms, winds, the history of forecasting, rain, sunny days, tales of the many times weather changed the course of history, and even extraterrestrial weather.
It’s time to grab your umbrella, don your sunglasses, and venture outdoors, whatever the weather.

_**Ideal for word geeks, weather buffs, and anybody who has ever moaned about the rain.**_

The [**pre-order for the Kindle edition is live now at this page**](link_9). Alternatively, hang on for the paperback and hardback editions – all coming on the 9th of November 2026. [**Signed copies can be ordered directly from me**](link_10).

Add it to your “Want to Read” list on [Goodreads](link_11). We’re working on getting this title into libraries too, watch this space.

* * *

[![Image 3: Modern Words with Old Roots](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/cover-ebook-small.jpeg?w=400)](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/cover-ebook-small.jpeg)**“Words Christmas Gave Us”** (2024) unwraps the stories behind the season, via festive words from _advent_ to _yule_ and _grinch_ to _scurryfunge_.

This book, the third in the series, explores the influence of Greeks, Romans, Vikings, Tudors, Dickens, and of course _Santa Claus_, on worldwide traditions, merry music, decorations, feasts, and more. Discover why Jean-Paul Sartre wrote a _nativity play_, when _Jingle Bells_ was sung in space, who gave us _gingerbread houses_, what Christmas _decoration_ used to contain false teeth, and how a newspaper typo started _Santa tracking_.

Pull on your Santa hat and dive into the words and history of Christmas.

_**Ideal for****word geeks, Christmas enthusiasts, and anybody who’s ever said Bah Humbug or Ho Ho Ho.**_

**Out now in Kindle, paperback, and hardback. If you’d like a signed bookplate – [check details here](link_12).**

*   [Signed copies available](link_10) direct from me to Ireland, UK, Europe, and other countries.
*   Available from independent bookshops – [Company of Books](link_13) Ranelagh Dublin, [Alan Hanna’s](link_14) Rathmines Dublin.
*   Irish or European Reader? [Amazon.ie](link_15), [Amazon.de](link_16) (click the flag to shop in English), [Book Delivery](link_17)
*   UK Reader? [Amazon.co.uk](link_18), [Waterstones](link_19), [Foyles](link_20),
*   American Reader? Try [Amazon.com](link_21), [ThriftBooks](link_22), [Bookshop.org](link_23), [Books A Million](link_24)
*   Italian? Try [Ibs](link_25)
*   Swedish? Try [Bokus.com](link_26), [Adlibris](link_27),
*   Danish? Try [Saxo](link_28)
*   New Zealand? Try [FishPond](link_30)
*   India? Try [BooksWagon](link_31)
*   Would you like a hardback? Available at [Amazon.ie](link_32), [Amazon.de,](link_33)[Amazon.uk,](link_34)[Amazon.com](link_35) etc.
*   Kindle on [Amazon.com](link_36), [Amazon.co.uk](link_37), [Amazon.de](link_38) etc.
*   Irish Library user? [**Search Grace Tierney on the Libraries Ireland website**](link_39) and you’ll find an up to date catalogue listing. Remember you can borrow my books from any library in Ireland via Inter Library Loan at your local branch. At March 2025 this book is available in paperback in six libraries.

Add it to your “Want to Read” list on [Goodreads](link_40). We’re working on getting this title into libraries too, watch this space.

**Reviews**

“This truly is a wonderful book for anyone who loves Christmas and/or words and their meanings and origins.” Marleen Kennedy, librarian and book blogger at The [Way She Reads](link_41).

“A veritable cornucopia of words that make Christmas for everyone.” Irene Gahan, writer and owner of the Academy [Bookshop.](link_42)

“The ideal Christmas present. International fun facts but also thought-provoking re how and why we do (and say) what we do (and say)!” [Jean Gill](link_43), historic fiction author.

* * *

[![Image 4](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/words-the-vikings-gave-us-cover-ps-4aug2021-1.jpg?w=212&h=327)](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/words-the-vikings-gave-us-cover-ps-4aug2021-1.jpg)

**“Words The Vikings Gave Us”** (2021) takes a light-hearted look at the horde of words the English dictionary stole from the Vikings. From _akimbo_ to _yule_ Old Norse merged with Anglo-Saxon to form the start of the English language.

This book, the second in the series, explores the Viking history of words like _kiss_, _ombudsman, bluetooth, frisbee, thing_, and _hustings_. _**More than 300 words and phrases**_ are featured – drawn from ship life, Viking food, farming, norse romance, myths, politics, modern Vikings, anatomy, place names, daily life, and of course _**how to fight like a Viking**_. It’s time to set sail in your longship. Horned helmet optional.

_**Ideal for word geeks, history buffs, and anybody who’s ever longed to throw an axe.**_

**Out now in paperback & ebook editions. If you’d like a signed bookplate – [check details here](link_12).**

*   [Signed copies available](link_10) direct from me to Ireland, UK, Europe, and other countries
*   Available from independent bookshops – [The Company of Books](link_44), Ranelagh, Dublin (€12.50)
*   Irish or European Reader? [Amazon.ie](link_45), [Amazon.de](link_46) €12.83 (click the flag to shop in English), [Book Delivery](link_47)
*   UK Reader? [Amazon.co.uk](link_48) £9.99, [Waterstones](link_49), [WHSmith](link_50), [Blackwells](link_51), [Hive](link_52), [World of Books](link_53)
*   American Reader? Try [Amazon.com](link_54) ($14.99), [Bookshop.org](link_55), and [Books A Million](link_56)
*   Swedish? Try [Bokus.com](link_57) (183kr)
*   New Zealand? [MightyApe](link_58), [FishPond](link_29)
*   [World of Books](link_59) worldwide
*   Irish Library user? [**Search Grace Tierney on the Libraries Ireland website**](link_39) and you’ll find an up to date catalogue listing. Remember you can borrow my books from any library in Ireland via Inter Library Loan at your local branch. At March 2025 this book is available in paperback in one library.

Available now in ebook format (c. $2.99)

*   Kindle on [Amazon.com](link_60), [Amazon.co.uk](link_61), [Amazon.de](link_46) etc.
*   [Kobo](link_62)

Add it to your “Want to Read” list on [Goodreads](link_63).

* * *

![Image 5: Modern Words Try 1 - 1](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/modern-words-final-cover-file.jpg?w=225&h=352)

**“Modern Words with Old Roots”** (2022). After four books, fourteen years of weekly articles, a radio show, and more dictionaries than you can throw a hat at, Wordfoolery takes a lighthearted look at the astonishingly ancient history of a hand-picked selection of **50 modern words** from _avatar_ to _zarf_.

It’s time to _login_ (inspired by an actual piece of wood), open your _kindle_ (inspired by Vikings), forget about the latest world _crisis_ (thanks to an ancient Greek doctor), skip the _doomscrolling_ (with a nod to William the Conqueror), and set off in _hot pursuit_ (from the Age of Sail) of some juicy language fact hunting. You may be surprised by what you discover.

Words change constantly, acquiring new meanings, and finding fans in new generations. This **digital exclusive** book rejoices in their evolution.

_**Ideal for word geeks, history buffs, and anybody who’s ever wondered about the roots of the latest trendy word in the dictionary.**_

**Reviews**

“Really good book” – Susie Dent, lexicographer and Queen of Dictionary Corner on Channel 4’s “Countdown”.

**Out now in ebook only**

*   Kindle on [Amazon.com](link_64) ($0.99), [Amazon.co.uk](link_65) (£0.99), [Amazon.de](link_66) (€0.99) etc.

Add it to your “Want to Read” list on Goodreads.

* * *

# [The Evil Roots of Malevolent](link_11)

[3 Replies](link_11)

Hello,

This week’s word is _malevolent_, not that I’m feeling particularly so this morning, just the average amount for a Monday morning (I agree with Garfield).

[![Image 3](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/grumpy-tiki.jpg?w=625)](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/grumpy-tiki.jpg)

“Grumpy Tiki” – a wood carving by my DH whose cantankerous face adorns our garden

_Malevolent_ is defined as wishing ill to others, being malicious, or ill will. It’s not the most pleasant of human traits and yet it’s one marked in many languages. Apparently Japanese has an expression which translates as “the misfortunes of others are sweet like honey” (ouch!), French has _joie maligne_, and the Germans gave us _Schadenfreude_. It appears that everybody likes to witness the downfall of others, at least sometimes.

_Malevolent_ is the English version of this and we have the Romans to thank for it. It arrived in English around 1500 from _malivolent_ in Old French and before that _malevolentem_ in Latin where it meant ill-disposed, spiteful, and envious. The word was formed in Latin from _male_ (badly) and _volentem_ (from the verb to wish). Basically if you directed bad wishes, as opposed to good wishes, towards somebody you were being _malevolent_. The word hasn’t changed in the centuries since, and sadly humans still harbour this emotion, especially on Mondays, at least according to Garfield.

If you’d like to do something positive rather than _malevolent_ today I’ll just remind you that **“Words the Weather Gave Us”**, my latest etymology book is coming on the 9th of November 2026 (all going to plan) but you **[can pre-order the Kindle ebook edition at this link here](link_12)**. As usual **[if you’re looking for a signed copy, get in touch with me](link_13)** via this page. Of course if you’re looking for an **Advance Review Copy** comment below and I’ll be in touch. If you’re on Goodreads, feel free to add it to your “Want To Read” list. Thanks!

Until next time, happy reading, writing, and wordfooling,

Grace ([@Wordfoolery](link_14))

# [Weather Book Cover and the History of Being Drenched](link_25)

[Leave a reply](link_25)

Hello,

I’m pleased to announce that **“Words the Weather Gave Us”**, the fourth book in [my Words series](link_26), is now available for pre-order (the ebook edition) and hence the cover is out too. Hope you like it? We went with a bright sunny look, but of course the book covers all types of weather.

[![Image 4](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/weather-ebook-cover-jpeg.jpg)](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/weather-ebook-cover-jpeg.jpg)

Words the Weather Gave Us

It explores delightful words like _petrichor, degombling, apricity, bumbershoot, dreich_, and _impluvious_ alongside words borrowed by English from all around the world. More than 330 words and phrases are featured – drawn from clouds, weather folklore and phrases, storms, winds, the history of forecasting, rain, sunny days, tales of the many times weather changed the course of history, and even extraterrestrial weather. I can’t wait to share it with you.

All three editions will be available from the 9th of November 2026 (all going to plan) but you **[can pre-order the Kindle ebook edition at this link here](link_12)**. As usual **[if you’re looking for a signed copy, get in touch with me](link_13)** via this page. Of course if you’re looking for an **Advance Review Copy**just comment below and I’ll be in touch.

The best way to explain the book is to share a few extracts so this week’s word is a weather one – drench.

**_Extract from “Words the Weather Gave Us” by Grace Tierney (copyright 2026)_**

Drench

This one I use often. If caught in a rain-shower unprepared and soaked through, I will announce “I’m drenched”. However an early user of English would then assume I had stopped by the pub on my walk.

Drench was drencan in Old English and it meant to ply with drink, to make drunk, to submerge, or to drown. The last meanings on that list work with the idea of rain clouds but the word’s roots lie in the verb drincan (to drink).

Drench has cousins in Old Norse, Swedish, Dutch, and German so all the northern Europeans were knocking back the ale and mead at that time. A friend might drench you the night before your wedding, for example.

It was the 1500s before drenching gained the idea of making somebody wet by throwing liquid over them but even in the word’s earlier days there was the idea of a drenc-flód which was a storm or a deluge.

The concept of drenching being forcing somebody to drink does linger however, in the idea of drenching farm animals with medicine.

**_{end of extract}_**

Until next time, happy reading, writing, and wordfooling,

Grace ([@Wordfoolery](link_14))

# [The Greek Word History of Ultracrepidarian](link_33)

[Leave a reply](link_33)

Hello,

Regular readers of the Wordfoolery blog ([and books](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/my-books/)) will know I love a good Greek etymology and that Greek gods and goddesses have a habit of sneaking into the back stories of various words. This week’s word, _ultracrepidarian_, a handily cryptic insult, which has Greek links but this time it’s not a deity who lies behind the story.

[![Image 5](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260914_111630.jpg?w=625)](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260914_111630.jpg)

Do you know somebody who likes to waffle on about a subject that they know nothing about? Most of us do. Well the next time they’re bothering you, try muttering _ultracrepidarian_. Don’t explain, just feel smug and remember this story. If they bustle off to look it up they may not even find it, unless they have a large dictionary as it’s not commonly used these days, but if they’re a true _ultracrepidarian_ they’re more likely to assume you’re admiring them, or that they already know the meaning.

_Ultracrepidarian_ entered English in 1819, more on that in a moment. Let’s explore its Greek roots first, with thanks to “Natural History” by Pliny the Elder who tells us about the first use. There was once a skilled artist called Apelles. He displayed his finished painting in public and lingered nearby to overhear the reactions. Like most creatives he was hoping for encouragement for his skill, but like most eavesdroppers he heard nothing good about himself.

A shoe-maker viewed the painting and criticised it on technical grounds, pointing out that the shoe (_crepida_) had the wrong number of straps. This was a fair comment and Apelles had the humility to correct the mistake overnight and then re-display the artwork.

The next day, however, the cobbler walked past again, and emboldened by having taught the mystery artist a lesson, decided to expand on his critique. He observed that the painting of the leg wasn’t good enough either. At this point Apelles stepped out of the crowd and said _“Ne sutor ultra crepidam”_ which translates as “Let the shoemaker not go beyond the sandal”. This advice to stick to his own area of expertise is one which is still needed at times, even today.

The expression became proverbial and via Latin was adopted into English as a noun, _ultracrepidarian_, in 1819 by the English essayist William Hazlitt. I studied some of his essays in school and I wish my teacher had told me this story back then. Hazlitt used it in an open letter to William Gifford, the editor of “The Quarterly Review” to criticise what he perceived to be over-reach.

The next time you are forced to listen to somebody talking confidently about a topic they really don’t know, hit them with _ultracrepidarian_. It might not stop them, but it should confuse them.

Until next time, happy reading, writing, and wordfooling,

Grace ([@Wordfoolery](link_14))

# [The Noisy Word History of Cliché](link_40)

[3 Replies](link_40)

Hello,

Last month I began writing **“Words Stories Gave Us”**, my book about the etymology of words from the worlds of stories, printing, newspapers, theatre, folktales, and books. I love this stage of a book when it’s all about searching out the stories, whittling out the boring ones, forming chapters. It will be a couple of years (aiming for 2028) before this one is on the shelves, but in the meantime I’ll share a word or two here as I work on them. Here’s the short story of the word _cliché_.

[![Image 6](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/printing-case.jpg?w=625)](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/printing-case.jpg)

Typesetter’s Case

**{Extract from “Words Stories Gave Us” by Grace Tierney, copyright 2026}**

**Cliché (this can also be spelled cliche)**

The last thing any writer wants to hear is that their work contains _clichés_. We want to (as the joke goes) avoid them like the plague. The problem is that some expressions or ideas are popular because they are meaningful, widely understood, and hence tempting to use, but they lack originality and impact.

It’s the idea of common use that gives us the word itself. That, and the world of printing presses. Although it didn’t become a popular English word until the 1920s, it joined English in the 1800s from _cliché_ in French. French printers used this term for a block of print which was used so often that you might as well keep it prepared and ready to go.

It’s believed that the word comes directly from the sound that print-block made as it _clicked_ into place, because the French verb _clicher_ means to _click_.

**{End of Extract}**

Until next time, happy reading, writing, and wordfooling,

Grace ([@Wordfoolery](link_14))

# Other Writing

I’ve been writing, and publishing worldwide since 2001. Here’s a selection of my clips. You can find details of my published books in [My Books](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/my-books/).

**Wordfoolery Whispers**

“Wordfoolery Whispers” provides the inside scoop on all of my writing, reading, and history adventures. Sneak peaks of new books, requests for help, contests, quizzes, and more. One per month because anything more is frankly annoying to you and me. You can subscribe now at **[subscribepage.io/wordfoolerywhispers](http://subscribepage.io/wordfoolerywhispers).**

**S****hort Fiction and Flash Fiction**

Various pieces for _Metro Fiction_, _The People’s Friend_, _E2K_, _Ireland’s Own_, and _StoryHouse Coffee_. Winner of the inaugural [Hinterland Festival](https://www.hinterland.ie/) Short Story Competition (2018).

**Blogging**

_Wordfoolery_ since 2009 (finalist and shortlisted in the Irish Blog Awards 2017, 2018).

Guest-blog series for the _[Irish Writer’s Centre](https://irishwriterscentre.ie/)_.

I helped judge the [Ireland Blog Awards](http://blogawardsireland.com/) 2018 (not in my category, of course).

**Non Fiction Articles, Editing, Staff Roles etc.**

_Prima_, _Your Family_, _The Irish Times Magazine_, _Food & Wine_, _Gardener’s World_, _The Dubliner_, _Funds for Writers_, _Vision_, and _Food Writing_.

My personal essays have featured in nine print anthologies.

Book reviews for _The Good Book Guide_ (staff), _Mid West Book Review_, _The Compulsive Reader_, _Women Writers_, _Crescent Blues_, and _Absolute Write_.

I’ve spoken at _Aghamore Literary Festival_ and[_Hinterland Literary Festival_](http://www.hinterland.ie/), and copy-edited two series of handbooks for _Scouting Ireland._

I’ve held staff positions at _Netsurfer Digest_, _The Good Book Guide_, _Writer Online_, and am a long-running columnist at [_The Meath Coaster_](https://www.meathcoaster.com/).

# Downloads

As a thank you to my readers this is where you will find snippets of my writing or extras available for download for reading or educational purposes. All are still copyright Grace Tierney but are free to download in pdf format. If you’d like to publish them online or in print, please contact me for permission. Just ask, I’ll probably say yes.

Happy reading!

**The History of Festoons & How to Crochet One ([Festoon pdf](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/festoon-history-and-crochet-pattern-pdf.pdf))**

While researching **“Words Christmas Gave Us”** I discovered the season is celebrated in many different ways worldwide and throughout history. You might roller-blade to church or use Crusader spices in your mince pies. Your Christmas carols could hide secret codes and hidden griefs or you could honour the Vikings by kissing under mistletoe. Anything goes.

I’ve gathered those stories into the book but as Christmas is a time for giving here’s the history of the word festoon through the ages. I hang several homemade festoons and paper-chains in my home each year so I’m including a crochet pattern to make your own from leftover yarn. It would make a wonderful gift. I hope you enjoy the story and the crafting inspiration.

If you enjoy the history of Christmas words, check out **“Words Christmas Gave Us”** out now in kindle, paperback, and hardback ([all the links to buy are here](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/my-books/)).

**The History of Gingerbread and Recipe ([Gingerbread pdf](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/gingerbread-history-and-recipe-pdf.pdf))**

I hope you enjoy this extract from my Christmas book about the history of Christmas gingerbread, with a little help from the Brothers Grimm and Crusading knights. I’ve included the recipe I use every Decemeber. If you enjoy the history of Christmas words, check out **“Words Christmas Gave Us”** out now in kindle, paperback, and hardback ([all the links to buy are here](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/my-books/)).

**Christmas Pudding History and Recipe for a Chocolate Version ([Pudding pdf](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/christmas-pudding-history-and-recipe-pdf.pdf))**

I hope you like this extract from my Christmas book about the long history of the Christmas pudding. The recipe changed a great deal over the centuries so if, like my family, you dislike dried fruit, why not try my recipe for a chocolate version. It’s a big hit in my house. If you enjoy the history of Christmas words, check out **“Words Christmas Gave Us”** out now in kindle, paperback, and hardback ([all the links to buy are here](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/my-books/)).

**Christmas Around the World ([Christmas around the world.pdf](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/christmas-around-the-world-pdf.pdf))**

The season is celebrated in different ways across the centuries and across the world. You might roller-blade to church in one country or use spices from the Crusades in your mince pies. You could wrap your gifts in fabric or sing carols with secret messages and hidden tales of grief. Christmas spiders could decorate your tree or you may honour Vikings by kissing under mistletoe. Festive traditions have deep, and global, roots. If you enjoy the history of Christmas words, check out **“Words Christmas Gave Us”** out now in kindle, paperback, and hardback ([all the links to buy are here](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/my-books/)).

**Words People and Places Gave Us ([People and Places](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/people-and-places.pdf "People and Places"))**

Since publishing **“How to Get Your Name in the Dictionary”** I’ve accumulated even more eponyms and toponyms. 57 of them are here, ranging from _silly billy_ to _tuxedo_ and _grinch_ to _mayonnaise_, along with their stories. You’ll discover how Chinese officials were linked to citrus fruits, why gloves were scented with almonds, how much _neanderthals_ loved poetry, and how a bitter rivalry between ancient libraries gave us _parchment_. If you discover you love these word histories – there are 260 more in [the original book, still available in ebook and paperback – all the buy links are here](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/my-books/).

**Nine Things You Never Knew About Vikings ([Viking pdf](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/nine-things-you-never-knew-about-vikings-pdf.pdf))**

While researching for “Words The Vikings Gave Us” I learned more about the Vikings than I ever did in school. Rather than turning my word history book into a ponderous tome on misunderstood Vikings, I’ve gathered some of my more surprising discoveries here. For example, their helmets didn’t have horns, the current Danish royals are descended from Vikings, Vikings discovered North America centuries before Columbus, and Vikings ruled Britain for four hundred years longer than the Romans. Plus they gave us the words hug, kiss, and glitter.

If you’re interested in Vikings you might enjoy my book **“Words The Vikings Gave Us”,**out now in ebook and paperback editions, [all the buy links are here](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/my-books/).

**Various Vessels ([Various Vessels pdf](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/various-vessels-pdf.pdf))**

It would be impossible to name and describe every vessel afloat but some ship names come laden with a cargo of romance and others evoke history. You may never need to identify the difference between a brigantine and a frigate but their stories are often intriguing. This article runs from _ark_ to y _awl_ and should help you navigate most marinas. If you enjoy nautical words you might enjoy my book **“Words The Sea Gave Us”**, out now in ebook and paperback editions, [all the buy links are here](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/my-books/).

# [Wordfoolery](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/ "Wordfoolery")

## Fooling with words since 2009

Menu[Skip to content](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/about/#content "Skip to content")

# About

**Media Kit & Blog Information**

**Author Biography**

I write in rural Ireland. I specialise in history and a humourous slant thanks to years of reading Wodehouse, Dickens, Pratchett, Brookmyre (see my three serialised novels on [Channillo](http://www.channillo.com/), the reading platform). My fiction and non-fiction has been published internationally and locally in everything from [the local paper](https://www.meathcoaster.com/) to anthologies, online media, coffee tins, and glossy magazines. I mentored the Ireland North East region in [NaNoWriMo](http://www.nanowrimo.org/) for 16 years. I’ve been blogging about the history of unusual words since 2009 and have published four books on the topic (“Words Christmas Gave Us”, “Words the Vikings Gave Us”, “Words The Sea Gave Us”, “How To Get Your Name In The Dictionary”). When I’m not writing, I read compulsively (I’m a top 60 reviewer in Ireland on [Goodreads](https://www.goodreads.com/author/show/18550070.Grace_Tierney), and am a Reading Ambassador for Ireland Reads Day) garden organically, crochet (find me on [Ravelry](https://www.ravelry.com/people/Gracetierney)), and hike. There aren’t many crafts I haven’t tried – my house is overflowing with creations.

**Contact Info**

*   email – grace at gracetierney dot com
*   bluesky – [https://bsky.app/profile/wordfoolery.bsky.social](https://bsky.app/profile/wordfoolery.bsky.social)
*   women on air [profile](https://womenonair.ie/commentator/grace-tierney/)
*   newsletter “Wordfoolery Whispers” [subscribepage.io/wordfoolerywhispers](http://subscribepage.io/wordfoolerywhispers)
*   what I’m reading [Bookbub](https://www.bookbub.com/profile/grace-tierney)&[Goodreads](https://www.goodreads.com/author/show/18550070.Grace_Tierney)
*   my social media links are on [my About.me profile](https://about.me/wordfoolery)

**Cover Images & Buy Links**

In side bar and on [My Books](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/my-books/) page

**Page Count, ISBN, Pricing**

“Words Christmas Gave Us”, 23 Sept 2024, 240 pages, ISBN 13 is 978-1999977672 €10.99/£9.99/$15.99 (paperback), 978-1999977696 €17.99/£15.99/$20.99 (hardback), 978-1999977689 €2.99/£2.50/$2.99 (kindle ebook).

“Words the Vikings Gave Us”, 14 Sept 2021, 224 pages, ISBN 13 is 978-1999977641, £9.99 UK paperback (£2.19 ebook), $14.99 US paperback ($2.99 ebook).

“Words the Sea Gave Us”, 13 July 2020, 280 pages, ISBN 13 is 978-1-9999776-2-7, £9.99 UK paperback (£2.27 ebook), $15.99 US paperback ($2.85 ebook).

“How To Get Your Name In The Dictionary”, 2018, 366 pages, ISBN 10 – 1999977602, £9.99 UK paperback (£2.27 ebook), $15.99 US paperback ($2.85 ebook).

**Author Image (available for use – reviews, articles etc.)**

![Image 2](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/graceauthorimage2018.jpg?w=625)

**Previous Interviews with Wordfoolery**

Feb 2025: [interview with AllAuthor about my writing process](https://allauthor.com/interview/gracetierney/).

You’ll find radio and podcast interviews on the [Listen to Wordfoolery page](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/listen-to-wordfoolery/).

Feb 2021: Wordfoolery talks about creativity during COVID lockdown to [Louth Libraries’ Shelf Life Blog](https://shelflifethelouthlibraryserviceblog.wordpress.com/2021/02/16/keepwell-part-six-creativity/)

June 2021: Wordfoolery chat about her books and creativity at [NFReads](https://www.nfreads.com/interview-with-author-grace-tierney/)

**Terms & Conditions “Stuff”**

While I am happy to guest blog, any text or images (unless otherwise noted) posted on this blog are copyright Grace Tierney. If you want to reblog, please contact me first for permission.

GDPR – I don’t gather anybody’s name, email, info via this blog. I certainly don’t store it or sell it. Two exceptions 1) I will keep your name if you suggest a word for the blog, or for my word books, so that I can give you a Thank You when I use it, 2) if you subscribe to Wordfoolery Whispers your email is retained so I can send you issues but you can unsubscribe at any time and I obey Mailerlite’s anti-spam rules.

My posts are my own opinion and are not paid for by any commercial entity. Since October 2018 I’ve included a small handful of affiliate links on books I recommend, particularly my own books, so I can earn a little towards the running costs of this blog. You don’t have to buy through those links, but if you do it would be helpful. As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases on Amazon.com.

**Ways You Can Support This Blog**

I blog because I love words. If you find the blog useful, or entertaining, feel free to support Wordfoolery in any of the following ways.

*   Buy [my books](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/my-books/)
*   Put a small tip in [my digital tip jar](https://ko-fi.com/G2G3DSRK)
*   Use [the affiliate links](https://ko-fi.com/G2G3DSRK) (& see sidebar) to go shopping, I get a small percentage back
*   Comment – reader feedback is priceless
*   [Suggest a word](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/nominate-a-word/)
*   Like or share my blog posts to your social media, I’d love more readers
*   Did I mention [buy my books](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/my-books/)?
*   You can now [Follow my blog with Bloglovin](https://www.bloglovin.com/blog/16067561/?claim=p9pau6mwj44)
*   Subscribe to “Wordfoolery Whispers” at [subscribepage.io/wordfoolerywhispers](http://subscribepage.io/wordfoolerywhispers)

### [Words The Sea Gave Us (Wordfoolery Words Series)](https://www.amazon.co.uk/gp/product/B08BK67ZYS?ref_=dbs_m_mng_rwt_calw_tkin_0&storeType=ebooks) (13 July 2020) 

 by [Grace Tierney (Author)](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Grace-Tierney/e/B07GSXVHZP?ref=dbs_mng_calw_a_0)

 4.9 [_4.9 out of 5 stars_ 11](https://www.amazon.co.uk/product-reviews/B08BK67ZYS/ref=dbs_r_series)

“Words The Sea Gave Us” is a light-hearted look at the words the English dictionary borrowed from the sea. From baggywinkle and gollywobbler to tempest and flotsam, the sea in all her moods has given a boatload of words to the English language throughout history. This book explores their origins along with a cargo of old sailor’s yarns. Cast your line for the salty history of skyscraper, mollgogger, strike, cyber, and phrases like getting hitched, red herring, hot pursuit, and taking them down a peg. More than 370 words and phrases are featured from “above board” to yardarm - drawn from parts of a ship, sail names, crew titles, surfer slang, marine monsters, nautical navigation, flying the flag, and of course, how to talk like a scurvy pirate. Throw in some sea fables, fashions, and weather and you’re ready to set sail. Previous nautical experience not required. Ideal for word geeks, sailors, and beachcombers.

# [The Evil Roots of Malevolent](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/2026/09/28/the-evil-roots-of-malevolent/)

[3 Replies](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/2026/09/28/the-evil-roots-of-malevolent/#comments)

Hello,

This week’s word is _malevolent_, not that I’m feeling particularly so this morning, just the average amount for a Monday morning (I agree with Garfield).

[![Image 2](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/grumpy-tiki.jpg?w=625)](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/grumpy-tiki.jpg)

“Grumpy Tiki” – a wood carving by my DH whose cantankerous face adorns our garden

_Malevolent_ is defined as wishing ill to others, being malicious, or ill will. It’s not the most pleasant of human traits and yet it’s one marked in many languages. Apparently Japanese has an expression which translates as “the misfortunes of others are sweet like honey” (ouch!), French has _joie maligne_, and the Germans gave us _Schadenfreude_. It appears that everybody likes to witness the downfall of others, at least sometimes.

_Malevolent_ is the English version of this and we have the Romans to thank for it. It arrived in English around 1500 from _malivolent_ in Old French and before that _malevolentem_ in Latin where it meant ill-disposed, spiteful, and envious. The word was formed in Latin from _male_ (badly) and _volentem_ (from the verb to wish). Basically if you directed bad wishes, as opposed to good wishes, towards somebody you were being _malevolent_. The word hasn’t changed in the centuries since, and sadly humans still harbour this emotion, especially on Mondays, at least according to Garfield.

If you’d like to do something positive rather than _malevolent_ today I’ll just remind you that **“Words the Weather Gave Us”**, my latest etymology book is coming on the 9th of November 2026 (all going to plan) but you **[can pre-order the Kindle ebook edition at this link here](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HJHVHC52?spcref=PUBLISHED_PREORDER_LIVE)**. As usual **[if you’re looking for a signed copy, get in touch with me](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/would-you-like-a-signed-copy/)** via this page. Of course if you’re looking for an **Advance Review Copy** comment below and I’ll be in touch. If you’re on Goodreads, feel free to add it to your “Want To Read” list. Thanks!

Until next time, happy reading, writing, and wordfooling,

Grace ([@Wordfoolery](https://twitter.com/Wordfoolery))

Don’t forget to click on the confirmation email, which might hide in your spam folder. Alternatively, check out **[my books about word histories](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/my-books/)**.

# [Weather Book Cover and the History of Being Drenched](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/2026/09/21/weather-book-cover-and-the-history-of-being-drenched/)

[Leave a reply](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/2026/09/21/weather-book-cover-and-the-history-of-being-drenched/#respond)

Hello,

I’m pleased to announce that **“Words the Weather Gave Us”**, the fourth book in [my Words series](https://www.amazon.co.uk/dp/B09C39L9VS), is now available for pre-order (the ebook edition) and hence the cover is out too. Hope you like it? We went with a bright sunny look, but of course the book covers all types of weather.

[![Image 3](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/weather-ebook-cover-jpeg.jpg)](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/weather-ebook-cover-jpeg.jpg)

Words the Weather Gave Us

It explores delightful words like _petrichor, degombling, apricity, bumbershoot, dreich_, and _impluvious_ alongside words borrowed by English from all around the world. More than 330 words and phrases are featured – drawn from clouds, weather folklore and phrases, storms, winds, the history of forecasting, rain, sunny days, tales of the many times weather changed the course of history, and even extraterrestrial weather. I can’t wait to share it with you.

All three editions will be available from the 9th of November 2026 (all going to plan) but you **[can pre-order the Kindle ebook edition at this link here](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HJHVHC52?spcref=PUBLISHED_PREORDER_LIVE)**. As usual **[if you’re looking for a signed copy, get in touch with me](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/would-you-like-a-signed-copy/)** via this page. Of course if you’re looking for an **Advance Review Copy**just comment below and I’ll be in touch.

The best way to explain the book is to share a few extracts so this week’s word is a weather one – drench.

**_Extract from “Words the Weather Gave Us” by Grace Tierney (copyright 2026)_**

Drench

This one I use often. If caught in a rain-shower unprepared and soaked through, I will announce “I’m drenched”. However an early user of English would then assume I had stopped by the pub on my walk.

Drench was drencan in Old English and it meant to ply with drink, to make drunk, to submerge, or to drown. The last meanings on that list work with the idea of rain clouds but the word’s roots lie in the verb drincan (to drink).

Drench has cousins in Old Norse, Swedish, Dutch, and German so all the northern Europeans were knocking back the ale and mead at that time. A friend might drench you the night before your wedding, for example.

It was the 1500s before drenching gained the idea of making somebody wet by throwing liquid over them but even in the word’s earlier days there was the idea of a drenc-flód which was a storm or a deluge.

The concept of drenching being forcing somebody to drink does linger however, in the idea of drenching farm animals with medicine.

**_{end of extract}_**

Until next time, happy reading, writing, and wordfooling,

# [The Noisy Word History of Cliché](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/2026/09/07/the-noisy-word-history-of-cliche/)

[3 Replies](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/2026/09/07/the-noisy-word-history-of-cliche/#comments)

Hello,

Last month I began writing **“Words Stories Gave Us”**, my book about the etymology of words from the worlds of stories, printing, newspapers, theatre, folktales, and books. I love this stage of a book when it’s all about searching out the stories, whittling out the boring ones, forming chapters. It will be a couple of years (aiming for 2028) before this one is on the shelves, but in the meantime I’ll share a word or two here as I work on them. Here’s the short story of the word _cliché_.

[![Image 4](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/printing-case.jpg?w=625)](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/printing-case.jpg)

Typesetter’s Case

**{Extract from “Words Stories Gave Us” by Grace Tierney, copyright 2026}**

**Cliché (this can also be spelled cliche)**

The last thing any writer wants to hear is that their work contains _clichés_. We want to (as the joke goes) avoid them like the plague. The problem is that some expressions or ideas are popular because they are meaningful, widely understood, and hence tempting to use, but they lack originality and impact.

It’s the idea of common use that gives us the word itself. That, and the world of printing presses. Although it didn’t become a popular English word until the 1920s, it joined English in the 1800s from _cliché_ in French. French printers used this term for a block of print which was used so often that you might as well keep it prepared and ready to go.

It’s believed that the word comes directly from the sound that print-block made as it _clicked_ into place, because the French verb _clicher_ means to _click_.

**{End of Extract}**

Until next time, happy reading, writing, and wordfooling,

Grace ([@Wordfoolery](https://twitter.com/Wordfoolery))

Grace Tierney writes in rural Ireland. Her award winning Wordfoolery blog about unusual English words has been running for 17 years exploring everything from "pooka" to "friggatriskaidekaphobia". Grace's favourite eponymous hero is Casanova because his swashbuckling life was so extraordinary, yet he ended up as a quiet librarian. Her favourite word from the sea is gollywobbler because it sounds silly. Her favourite Viking words are hug (so unexpected!) and attercop from her beloved childhood book "The Hobbit". Her favourite Christmas word is twixtmas because she loves that peaceful family time between Christmas and New Year's Eve. For weather words she loves degombling and dreich.

When not writing you'll find her reading, crafting, or hiking up a hill.

This book, the third in the series, explores the influence of Greeks, Romans, Vikings, Tudors, Dickens, and of course _Santa Claus_, on worldwide traditions, merry music, decorations, feasts, and more. Discover why Jean-Paul Sartre wrote a _nativity play_, when _Jingle Bells_ was sung in space, who gave us _gingerbread houses_, what Christmas _decoration_ used to contain false teeth, and how a newspaper typo started _Santa tracking_.

Pull on your Santa hat and dive into the words and history of Christmas.

_**Ideal for****word geeks, Christmas enthusiasts, and anybody who’s ever said Bah Humbug or Ho Ho Ho.**_

**“Words The Vikings Gave Us”** (2021) takes a light-hearted look at the horde of words the English dictionary stole from the Vikings. From _akimbo_ to _yule_ Old Norse merged with Anglo-Saxon to form the start of the English language.

This book, the second in the series, explores the Viking history of words like _kiss_, _ombudsman, bluetooth, frisbee, thing_, and _hustings_. _**More than 300 words and phrases**_ are featured – drawn from ship life, Viking food, farming, norse romance, myths, politics, modern Vikings, anatomy, place names, daily life, and of course _**how to fight like a Viking**_. It’s time to set sail in your longship. Horned helmet optional.

_**Ideal for word geeks, history buffs, and anybody who’s ever longed to throw an axe.**_

![Image 5: Modern Words Try 1 - 1](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/modern-words-final-cover-file.jpg?w=225&h=352)

**“Modern Words with Old Roots”** (2022). After four books, fourteen years of weekly articles, a radio show, and more dictionaries than you can throw a hat at, Wordfoolery takes a lighthearted look at the astonishingly ancient history of a hand-picked selection of **50 modern words** from _avatar_ to _zarf_.

It’s time to _login_ (inspired by an actual piece of wood), open your _kindle_ (inspired by Vikings), forget about the latest world _crisis_ (thanks to an ancient Greek doctor), skip the _doomscrolling_ (with a nod to William the Conqueror), and set off in _hot pursuit_ (from the Age of Sail) of some juicy language fact hunting. You may be surprised by what you discover.

Words change constantly, acquiring new meanings, and finding fans in new generations. This **digital exclusive** book rejoices in their evolution.

_**Ideal for word geeks, history buffs, and anybody who’s ever wondered about the roots of the latest trendy word in the dictionary.**_

[**“Words The Sea Gave Us”**](https://amzn.to/37RQffU) (2020) is a light-hearted look at the words the English dictionary borrowed from the sea. From _baggywinkle_ and _gollywobbler_ to _tempest_ and _flotsam_, the sea in all her moods has given a boatload of words to the English language throughout history. This book explores their origins along with a cargo of old sailor’s yarns. Cast your line for the salty history of _skyscraper, mollgogger, strike, cyber_, and phrases like _getting hitched, red herring, hot pursuit,_ and _taking them down a peg_.

More than _**370 words and phrases**_ are featured from _above board_ to _yardarm_ – drawn from parts of a ship, sail names, crew titles, surfer slang, marine monsters, nautical navigation, flying the flag, and of course,_**how to talk like a scurvy pirate**_. Throw in some sea fables, fashions, and weather and you’re ready to set sail.

Previous nautical experience not required.

_**Ideal for word geeks, sailors, and beachcombers.**_

These heroes and heroines, scattered through world history, all did something extraordinary to squeeze their name into the dictionary, and this book celebrates their biographies.

More than **_260 eponyms_** are featured across subjects as diverse as food, Irish history, calendars, hats, inventions, words named after places, Greek gods, military history, politics, astronomy, fashion, popular phrases, villains, science, and a selection of eponyms which simply defy categorisation.

# The Obscure Origins of the Game of Poker

[1 Reply](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/2020/10/12/the-obscure-origins-of-the-game-of-poker/#comments)

Hello,

This morning, for some strange reason, my mind is on the game of _poker_. Not the _poker_ you use to stir up your fire (which dates to the 1530s in English and yes, it does relate to being a object used to _poke_ the fire).

As I’ve found before when looking at words around card playing, there’s little definitive clarity to be found when it comes to _poker_. This seems appropriate to me as a total _poker_ amateur. On the rare nights when our family sits down for a game we all have to refer to the sheet of rules on which hands beat others. I suspect this means we would be easy prey for any hustler in a hundred mile radius. Luckily we play only for the plastic chips, and the bragging rights of being the winner.

[![Image 2](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/poker.jpg?w=1024)](https://wordfoolery.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/poker.jpg)

Sadly this is not the hand I usually get when playing

Bragging is appropriate as it turns out. An earlier version of the game was called _Brag_. I think I recall them playing it in Jane Austen novels?

Even if you’ve never played a hand of _poker_ in earnest I’m sure you’ve seen it played in movies – by cowboys in a saloon, gangsters in a back room, or grifters in a casino. The game first appeared around the late 1820s, perhaps starting amongst riverboat gamblers on the great Mississippi river. As a result the word entered English with thanks to the Americans.

It wasn’t entirely American however. There was an earlier card game called _Pochspiel_ in German. _Spiel_ means play or game, and the _Poch_ part of the word comes from _pochen_(the verb to brag or bluff). There may even have been a French game called _poque_ which was very similar. It appears that several countries had card games involving bluffing around the same time period and any of them could have been the original source but the American gamblers slipped the word into mainstream English usage and usually take credit on this one. Whist, another very popular card game (this time taught to me by a nun in the 1980s!) also involves bluffing and it dates back to the 1660s, so _poker_ isn’t the first by any means.

The related term is, of course, _poker face_. Early examples of its use to describe somebody controlling their facial expressions to improve their chances in the game date back to the 1870s. This is something I’ve yet to achieve so it’s probably best that I stick to playing with plastic chips rather than cash.

Until next time happy reading, writing, and wordfooling,

Grace ([@wordfoolery](https://twitter.com/Wordfoolery))

Luana Costa 24 Mar 2026](https://explore.theskindeep.com/what-we-keep-learning-from-the-and/)[![Image 5: a film set with lights, cameras, and two chairs](https://storage.ghost.io/c/f4/72/f4726e04-2cb7-41b7-8978-c308ea31ab1d/content/images/size/w720/2026/01/20260110_073156-1-1.jpg) ### Behind The Scenes: The Skin Deep New Orleans If you take one thing away from this, let it be this: an incredible amount of time, effort, love, and care goes into each production. ## THE SKIN DEEP: CHANGING THE WORLD ONE CONVERSATION AT A TIME

We create the space for people to experience deeper connection with the most important people in their lives.

Our journey began with a simple premise: to film authentic and emotional conversations between two people as they asked intimate questions and invited viewers into their emotional space. It was a risky endeavor, but we believed in the power of human connection and the need for genuine human interaction.

When our first project, {THE AND}, became an instant global hit, garnering 55 million views and earning us an Emmy-Award, we knew that we had created something truly special.

Since 2014, we have produced over 1,200 honest and authentic conversations in locations around the world, documenting human connection in all its forms through the format of {THE AND}. The project has grown from video, to live events, an app, podcast series and card games in 12 editions and multiple languages loved by millions of people around the world.

We’ve seen over and over again that creating the space for intimate conversation and asking well constructed questions unlocks magic between people.

**Our mission is to create experiences that allow more people to have deep, cathartic conversations, explore their relationship and experience deeper connection.**

_Why?_

We believe that unlocking the power of deeper human connection can transform our relationships, our lives and our society.

By amplifying and illuminating our shared humanity, we can create a more compassionate and empathetic world.

We continue to dedicate ourselves to this pursuit.

 Description 

**Bored of the same old routine with your person? Time to keep each other guessing.**

You know that feeling when someone catches you completely off guard and you can't stop laughing? Kidulting is built to manufacture that on purpose. It's a card game for two — each of you gets a deck, and you spring ridiculous prompts on each other over any timeframe you like. Sing a song of their choice. Invent three yoga poses on the spot. Talk only in emoji until dinner. It's permission for the two of you to be gloriously, harmlessly twelve again.

**What's in the Box?**

*   100 delightfully ridiculous prompts across two decks — one for each of you
*   A game with no board, no timer, and no winner — just the two of you and the chaos you agree to
*   Prompts you can spring in a single night or stretch across weeks
*   Silly, surprising, laugh-out-loud fun — never vulgar, never spicy, never awkward

**Why Kidulting Hits Different:**

1.   **It catches them off guard.** The magic isn't playing a round — it's dropping a card mid-breakfast, mid-errand, mid-Tuesday. Every prompt turns an ordinary moment into a story you'll both retell.
2.   **You play it your way.** One card or the whole deck. All in one evening or over a month. You set the pace, the timeframe, and exactly how much dignity you're willing to sacrifice.
3.   **It's silly, never spicy.** No vulgar cards, no suggestive stuff, nothing you'd wince at. Just genuinely funny, wonderfully absurd challenges any two people can play.
4.   **It's the lighthearted one from The Skin Deep.** From the makers of {THE AND}, the conversation game with over half a million sold. When {THE AND} goes deep, Kidulting keeps it light — same two people, pure silliness instead of big questions.
5.   **Zero learning curve.** No rulebook, no setup. Pick a card, spring it, play. That's the whole game.

**Who's It For?**

*   Couples who want more laughing and less scrolling in their day-to-day
*   Any two people who spend a lot of time together: roommates, best friends, siblings
*   Anyone hunting for a gift that actually gets played, not shelved
*   Duos who refuse to take life too seriously
*   People who love {THE AND} and want the goofy counterpart to it

**Stop Scrolling. Start Playing.**

Every ordinary week is one you could've turned into a running joke between the two of you. Grab Kidulting, pick a card, and spring it when they least expect it.

_Warning: May cause uncontrollable laughter, a stronger bond with your person, and a lingering urge to get them back the moment they get you. Side effects include ordinary Tuesdays becoming unforgettable and neither of you ever seeing the next card coming._

## THE SKIN DEEP: CHANGING THE WORLD ONE CONVERSATION AT A TIME

Our journey began with a simple premise: to film authentic and emotional conversations between two people as they asked intimate questions and invited viewers into their emotional space. It was a risky endeavor, but we believed in the power of human connection and the need for genuine human interaction.

When our first project, {THE AND}, became an instant global hit, garnering 55 million views and earning us an Emmy-Award, we knew that we had created something truly special.

Since 2014, we have produced over 1,200 honest and authentic conversations in locations around the world, documenting human connection in all its forms through the format of {THE AND}. The project has grown from video, to live events, an app, podcast series and card games in 12 editions and multiple languages loved by millions of people around the world.

We’ve seen over and over again that creating the space for intimate conversation and asking well constructed questions unlocks magic between people.

**Our mission is to create experiences that allow more people to have deep, cathartic conversations, explore their relationship and experience deeper connection.**

_Why?_

We believe that unlocking the power of deeper human connection can transform our relationships, our lives and our society.

By amplifying and illuminating our shared humanity, we can create a more compassionate and empathetic world.

We continue to dedicate ourselves to this pursuit.

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Baraja_de_UNO.JPG/250px-Baraja_de_UNO.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Baraja_de_UNO.JPG)

Old Uno cards

**Uno** ([/ˈ uː n oʊ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[](link_6)[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LL-Q1860_(eng)-Flame,_not_lame-Uno_(card_game).wav "File:LL-Q1860 (eng)-Flame, not lame-Uno (card game).wav"); from [Spanish](link_7) and [Italian](link_8) for 'one'), stylized in [all caps](link_9) as **UNO**, is a proprietary American [shedding-type card game](link_10) originally developed in 1971 by [Merle Robbins](link_4) in [Reading, Ohio](link_11), a [suburb](link_12) of [Cincinnati](link_13), that housed International Inc., a gaming company acquired by [Mattel](link_5) on January 23, 1992.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-2)

The game is played with a [dedicated deck](link_14) derived from the [crazy eights](link_15) family of card games which, in turn, is based on the traditional German game of [mau-mau](link_16).

## History

The game was originally developed in 1971 by [Merle Robbins](link_4) in [Reading, Ohio](link_11), a suburb of [Cincinnati](link_13). When his family and friends began to play more and more, he and his family mortgaged their home to raise $8,000 to have 5,000 copies of the game made.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-3) He sold it from his [barbershop](link_17) at first, and local businesses began to sell it as well. Robbins later sold the rights to Uno to a group of friends headed by Robert Tezak, a funeral parlor owner in [Joliet, Illinois](link_18), for $50,000 plus royalties of 10 cents per game. Tezak formed International Games, Inc., to market Uno, with offices behind his funeral parlor. The games were produced by Lewis Saltzman of Saltzman Printers in [Maywood, Illinois](link_19).

In 1992, International Games became part of the [Mattel](link_5) family of companies.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-instructions2001-4)

In 2018, Uno was inducted into the [National Toy Hall of Fame](link_20) alongside [pinball](link_21) and the [Magic 8 Ball](link_22).[[5]](

M. (AP) — Bob Odenkirk is back shooting “Better Call Saul," six weeks after having a heart attack. Odenkirk on Wednesday tweeted a photo of himself getting made up to play title character Saul Goodman in the AMC series, indicating that shooting had resumed on its sixth and final season. “Back to work on Better Call Saul! ” Odenkirk said. “So happy to be here and living this specific life surrounded by such good people.](https://kfoxtv.com/news/entertainment/bob-odenkirk-back-on-better-call-saul-after-heart-attack [link_7])

[![Image 12](https://kfoxtv.com/resources/media2/16x9/full/260/center/80/4dca32b4-fe66-4c7a-8db7-7e0ee31e1785-medium16x9_AP21209167451479.jpg) 5 years ago Bob Odenkirk collapses on 'Better Call Saul' set LOS ANGELES (AP) — “Better Call Saul” star Bob Odenkirk had a “heart related incident” when he collapsed on the show's New Mexico set, and his condition is stable as he recovers at a hospital, his representatives said Wednesday. “We can confirm Bob is in stable condition after experiencing a heart related incident," the statement said.](https://kfoxtv.com/news/entertainment/bob-odenkirk-collapses-on-better-call-saul-set [link_8])

[![Image 13](https://kfoxtv.com/resources/media2/16x9/full/260/center/80/4e62b650-c381-4357-9dbf-7d16ce878327-medium16x9_vlcsnap2019111907h54m27s947.png) 6 years ago Nonpartisan Uno encourages family fun without the politics Mattel is selling a new nonpartisan version of the card game Uno. It encourages families to gather at Thanksgiving and forget about politics. Nonpartisan Uno replaces red and blue cards -- which might be seen as politically charged -- with orange and purple. It also comes in a purple box, instead of the usual red. If someone starts talking politics while playing, anyone can grab the new "veto" card and play it to skip that person's turn.](https://kfoxtv.com/news/offbeat/nonpartisan-uno-encourages-family-fun-without-the-politics [link_9])

[![Image 14](https://kfoxtv.com/resources/media2/16x9/full/260/center/80/99cb17fe-c17f-4736-b99e-622ad6b962d8-medium16x9_AP18264721687011.jpg) 8 years ago A dog's life: Uno, beagle who wowed Westminster, dies at 13 Every dog might have its day, but not many ever had a night like this. Cheered on by a roaring, packed crowd at Madison Square Garden, the playful beagle responded like a true champ. "Ah-roo! " Uno bayed that evening, a decade ago. "Ah-roo! " Uno, who became perhaps the most popular pooch to step into a dog show ring, has died. He was 13. From a president to parades to ballparks, Uno charmed admirers wherever he wandered. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American inventor of the card game UNO

**Merlin "Merle" Robbins** (September 12, 1911 – January 14, 1984) was an American [barber](link_3) from [Reading, Ohio](link_4), who invented the [card game](link_5)[UNO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game) "Uno (card game)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Robbins#cite_note-obit-1) In 1971, he invented UNO to resolve an argument with his son Ray, a teacher, about the rules of [Crazy Eights](link_6).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Robbins#cite_note-2) The original decks were designed and made on the family dining room table. He and his family mortgaged their home to raise $8,000 and created the first 5,000 UNO decks to sell. At first, he sold them from his barber shop, while his son Ray gave them away to his students. In 1972, he sold the rights to UNO to International Games for $50,000 plus [royalties](link_7) of 10 cents per game.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Robbins#cite_note-obit-1)

Toy giant [Mattel](link_8) produces the game in 80 countries and, by 2006, had sold over 150 million copies worldwide.  Robbins died in 1984 in [Cincinnati, Ohio](link_9). He was 72.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Robbins#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Robbins#cite_note-4)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [Crazy eights](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Crazy_eights&redirect=no "Crazy eights"))

Card game

For other uses, see [Crazy Eights (disambiguation)](link_4).

"8s" and "8's" redirect here. For the numeral, see [8](link_5). For other uses, see [8 (disambiguation)](link_6) and [8S (disambiguation)](link_7).

Crazy Eights[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Crazy_Eights.jpg/250px-Crazy_Eights.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Crazy_Eights.jpg)

In Crazy Eights, playing an 8 card will change the current suit of the game.
Type Shedding
Players 2+
Skills[Tactics](link_8) and communication
Cards 52 (originally 28)
Deck[French](link_9)
Play Clockwise and counter-clockwise
Playing time Various
Chance Medium
Related games
[Mau Mau](link_10)•[Uno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game) "Uno (card game)")•[Whot](link_11)

**Crazy Eights** is a [card game](link_12) for two to seven players and the best known American member of the Eights Group which also includes [Switch](link_21), [Mau-Mau](link_13), [Whot!](link_14), and [Uno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game) "Uno (card game)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights#cite_note-parlett-1). The object of the game is to be the first player to discard all of their cards.

Originally this was played primarily by children with the left over cards not used in [Euchre](link_15). Now a [standard 52-card deck](link_16) is used when there are five or fewer players. When there are more than five players, two decks are shuffled together and all 104 cards are used.

## Origins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Crazy_Eights&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Origins")]

The game first appeared as _Eights_ in the 1930s,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights#cite_note-parlett-1) and the name _Crazy Eights_ dates to the 1940s, derived from the [United States](link_17) military designation for discharge of mentally unstable soldiers, [Section 8](link_18).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights#cite_note-3) It may have derived from the German game of [Mau-Mau](link_10).

There are many variations of the basic game, under names including _[Craits](link_19)_, _[Last card](link_20)_, and _[Switch](link_21)_. [Bartok](link_22), [Mao](link_23), [Taki](link_24), and [Uno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game) "Uno (card game)") add further elements to the game.

[David Parlett](link_25) describes Crazy Eights as "not so much a game as a basic pattern of play on which a wide variety of changes can be rung," noting that players can easily invent and explore new rules.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights#cite_note-parlett-1)

## Basic play

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Crazy_Eights&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Basic play")]

Five cards are dealt to each player (or seven in a two-player game).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights#cite_note-pagat-4) The remaining cards of the deck are placed face down at the center of the table as the stock pile. The top card is then turned face up to start the game as the first card in the discard pile.

Players discard by matching rank or suit with the top card of the discard pile, starting with the player left of the dealer. They can also play any 8 at any time, which allows them to declare the suit that the next player is to play; that player must then follow the named suit or play another 8. If a player is unable to play, that player draws cards from the stock pile until a play can be made, or until the stock pile is exhausted. If the player cannot play when the stock pile is exhausted, that player must pass the turn to the player on the left. Other variations have players limit the maximum number of cards drawn. A player may draw from the stock pile at any time, even when holding one or more playable cards.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights#cite_note-5)

As an example: If the top card on the discard pile is 6♣, the next player can:

1.   play any 6 (i.e. 6♦, 6♥ or 6♠)
2.   play any club
3.   play any 8, then declare a new suit
4.   draw from the stockpile until a play can be made

If the stock pile runs out, all played cards except for the top one are reshuffled to form a new stock.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights#cite_note-pagat-4)

The game ends as soon as one player has emptied their hand. That player collects a payment from each opponent equal to the point score of the cards remaining in that opponent's hand. 8s score 50, [court cards](link_26) 10 and all other cards face value. If the players run out of cards in the deck, the player with the lowest point score in their hand scores the difference between that hand and each opponent's hand.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights#cite_note-parlett-1)

The winner of the game is the first player to reach a specific number of points. The number of points needed to win is calculated by multiplying the number of players by 50. So, for two players it is 100 points, three players 150, four 200, five 250, six 300 and for seven players 350.

## Variations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Crazy_Eights&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Variations")]

Card game historian [John McLeod](link_27) describes Crazy Eights as "one of the easiest games to modify by adding variations",[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights#cite_note-pagat-4) and many variant rules exist. Common rules applied to cards include:

Queens skip Playing a Queen causes the next player to miss their turn.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights#cite_note-pagat-4)Aces reverse direction Playing an Ace reverses the direction of play.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights#cite_note-pagat-4)Draw 2 Playing a two forces the next player to draw two cards, unless they can play another two. Multiple twos "stack"; if a two is played in response to a two, the next player must draw four.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights#cite_note-pagat-4)
If the game ends on a special card, that card's rule is not applied.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights#cite_note-pagat-4)

A popular variant of the game in the United States is **Crazy Eights Countdown**, where players start with a score of 8. A player's score determines how many cards they are dealt at the start of each round, and which rank of card is wild for them. (So initially, all players are dealt eight cards and 8s are wild for everyone; after one round, one player will be dealt seven cards and 7s will be wild for them, but 8s will be wild for everyone else.) The first player to reduce their score to zero wins the game.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights#cite_note-pagat-4)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Hall of Fame in Rochester, New York

National Toy Hall of Fame[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Strong_national_museum_of_play_sculpture_%2825751934112%29.jpg/250px-Strong_national_museum_of_play_sculpture_%2825751934112%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Strong_national_museum_of_play_sculpture_(25751934112).jpg)

Entrance to The Strong, location of  
the Toy Hall of Fame
[![Image 5: Map](https://maps.wikimedia.org/img/osm-intl,13,a,a,250x200.png?lang=en&domain=en.wikipedia.org&title=National_Toy_Hall_of_Fame&revid=1368256544&groups=_5938b605c54be78d1706f1da373248104b6b3977&parser=parsoid)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Toy_Hall_of_Fame)
Established 1998;28 years ago(1998)
Location[The Strong](link_4), [Rochester, NY](link_5)
Type[Hall of Fame](link_6)
Collections[Toys](link_7)
Website[museumofplay.org/toy-hall-of-fame](https://www.museumofplay.org/exhibits/toy-hall-of-fame/)

The **National Toy Hall of Fame** is a U.S. [hall of fame](link_6) that recognizes the contributions of [toys](link_7) and [games](link_8) that have sustained their popularity for many years. Criteria for induction include: icon status (the toy is widely recognized, respected, and remembered); longevity (more than a passing fad); discovery (fosters learning, creativity, or discovery); and innovation (profoundly changed play or toy design).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Toy_Hall_of_Fame#cite_note-Hall_of_Famers:_Easy-Bake,_Lionel-1) Established in 1998 under the direction of Ed Sobey, it was originally housed at [A. C. Gilbert's Discovery Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._C._Gilbert [link_9]'s_Discovery_Village "A. C. Gilbert's Discovery Village") in [Salem, Oregon](link_10), [United States](link_11),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Toy_Hall_of_Fame#cite_note-2) but was moved to the [Strong National Museum of Play](link_12) (now [The Strong](link_4)) in [Rochester, New York](link_5), in 2002 after it outgrew its original home.

As of 2025, 91 toys have been enshrined in the National Toy Hall of Fame:

## Original inductees (1998-99)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Toy_Hall_of_Fame&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Original inductees (1998-99)")]

The original inductees to the National Toy Hall of Fame were announced in November 1999. Students from nearby [Willamette University](link_13) protested (good-naturedly) when they learned that [Mr. Potato Head](link_14) and [Barbie's friend Ken](link_15) were not included.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Toy_Hall_of_Fame#cite_note-via-3)

# Kelvin Waves are coming to California! So, what's a Kelvin Wave?

* * *

by Kris Kuyper

Sat, October 3, 2026 at 4:00 AM

![Image 7: UserWay icon for accessibility widget](https://kmph.com/resources/defaults/news_3.0/icons/accessibility/userway-transparent.svg)

It's this year's exciting new weather term: Kelvin Wave. I've noticed a number of articles online lately about how a Kelvin Wave is coming to California, and will raise the sea level. And it won't be just one - we can expect multiple Kelvin Waves this winter. So, what exactly is a Kelvin Wave, and should you be worried?

First - this has happened many times before, and will happen again in the future. It's a little like the term 'Polar Vortex' suddenly becoming popular around 10 years ago - it's a meteorological term that's been around forever, but suddenly became a huge 'buzz' word, and still is. But it's nothing new.

A Kelvin Wave is an underwater ocean wave (somewhat similar to a tsunami, but MUCH smaller and much longer lasting) that can raise the local sea level around 4" to 6" for roughly 1 to 3 weeks. Another rough analogy would be like a very small but much longer lasting Storm Surge. This would obviously have no impact on the San Joaquin Valley - only the coastline.

It often stems from El Niño . The Trade Winds at the Equatorial Pacific blow very steadily to the east, for years at a time. But when an El Niño develops, they shut down... and all that warm ocean water in the western Pacific suddenly sloshes back westward, towards South America. The water bounces off of South America, with some of it moving south, and some of it moving northward to California. When it arrives at the California coast, that surge of water raises the ocean level a few inches for a few weeks.

That alone doesn't sound like too much to worry about... but that's not all.

[Video 1](https://video.primis.tech/uploads/cn1/video/users/hls/31849/video_686d0ef5b52b9170515911/vid6ac0777740a48091963104.mp4/chunklist_480.m3u8)

This Kelvin Wave came from the Tropics, so it's warm water... definitely warmer than the usual cool Pacific Ocean off of California. We know from meteorology that cool air contracts and warm air expands... and the same principle of thermodynamics applies here to the ocean. The warmer water from the Kelvin Wave expands a little (called 'Thermal Expansion'), and that can add _**another**_ 4" to 8" of local sea level rise. That now brings the rise to potentially around 1 foot. With all of this happening during an El Niño winter, there may be strong storms - they can add another few inches of Storm Surge on top of the Kelvin Wave. Any wave action is going to happen on top of all of this, which might become destructive enough to cause serious damage to some restaurant on a pier, erode the hillside below nice homes on the coastline, or wash away tons of sand from a popular beach.

[Video 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PYxAWWtyIeg)

**Above:**Breaking down what an oceanic Kelvin Wave is, and it's possible impacts on California.

These waves are named after Lord Kelvin, who was a British Physicist and Mathematician in the 1800's who worked out the physics of these waves. He also has the Kelvin temperature scale named after him, which is the same as Celsius, except there are no negative numbers on the Kelvin scale. It begins at -273 C, which is absolute zero - the lowest temperature possible. So, 0 K is -273 C or -460 F. My father was an aerospace engineer, and he used the Kelvin scale for some of his work on spacecraft. The general temperature of space is about 3 K - very, very cold.

JOIN THE CONVERSATION (2)

Wave action from big Winter storms can destroy piers, erode coastal cliffs, and move tons of beach sand. The 1982/83 El Niño caused an estimate $14 million in damage to the California coastline, but the similar strength 1997/98 El Niño caused only half that. Planners learned weaknesses on the coast from the 1982/83 El Niño, and strengthened known weak spots. They also just got a bit lucky: some of the stronger storms on the 1997/98 El Niño peaked during low tide, while the opposite happened more often during the 1982/83 El Niño.
