**David Parlett** (born 18 May 1939 in London)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-1) is a games scholar, historian,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-2) and translator from South London, who has studied both [card games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Card_game "Card game")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-3) and [board games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_game "Board game").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-5) He is the president of the [British Skat Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Skat_Association "British Skat Association").

## Life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_Parlett&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

David Sidney Parlett was born in London on 18 May 1939 to Sidney Thomas Parlett and Eleanor May Parlett, née Nunan. He is one of three brothers. During the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Parlett lived in [Barry, Glamorgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry,_Vale_of_Glamorgan "Barry, Vale of Glamorgan"). He was educated at [Battersea Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battersea_Grammar_School "Battersea Grammar School") and the [University College of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_University "Aberystwyth University") in [Aberystwyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth "Aberystwyth"). He has a BA in Modern Languages. Parlett was a technical writer with PR companies and later a freelance writer for _Games & Puzzles_ magazine. He is married to Barbara and they have a son and a daughter.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-6)

## Works

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_Parlett&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Works")]

His published works include many popular books on games such as _Penguin Book of Card Games_,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-7) as well as the more academic volumes _The Oxford Guide to Card Games_ and _The Oxford History of Board Games_,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-8) both now out of print. Parlett has also invented many card games and board games. The most successful of these is _[Hare and Tortoise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hare\_and\_Tortoise "Hare and Tortoise")_ (1974). Its German edition was awarded [Spiel des Jahres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiel_des_Jahres "Spiel des Jahres") (Game of the Year) in 1979.

Parlett is a [Quaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers "Quakers").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-9)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_Parlett&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Board games")]

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [Mau Mau (card game)](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mau_Mau_(card_game)&redirect=no "Mau Mau (card game)"))

Card game

Not to be confused with [Mao (card game)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_(card_game) "Mao (card game)").

Mau-Mau[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Walet_Karo_z_Wzoru_Berli%C5%84skiego.png/120px-Walet_Karo_z_Wzoru_Berli%C5%84skiego.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Walet_Karo_z_Wzoru_Berli%C5%84skiego.png)

[Switch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switch_(card_game) "Switch (card game)")•[Crazy Eights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_Eights "Crazy Eights")•[Whot!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whot! "Whot!")

**Mau-Mau** is a [card game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Card_game "Card game") for two or more players that is popular in [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria"), [South Tyrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Tyrol "South Tyrol"), the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece"), [Czech Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Republic "Czech Republic"), [Slovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia "Slovakia"), [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel"), and the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"). Mau-Mau is a member of the [shedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Card_games#Shedding_games "Card games") family, to which the game [Crazy Eights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_Eights "Crazy Eights") with the proprietary card game [Uno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game) "Uno (card game)") belongs. Other similar games are [Whot!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whot! "Whot!") or [Switch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switch_(card_game) "Switch (card game)"). However, Mau-Mau is played with standard French or German-suited playing cards.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mau-Mau_(card_game)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Mau-Mau surfaced in Germany shortly after the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"). In 1961, it was still "a very recent game" that had gained "astonishing popularity within just a few years".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Mau_(card_game)#cite_note-Trumpf61-1)

Its rules were first published in 1958 and although "it appeared quite suddenly... anyone who has played it once will be enthralled by it... Its particular charm lies in its cheerful, light entertaining character and perfectly refined simplicity. Anyone can play it in five minutes".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Mau_(card_game)#cite_note-Trumpf58-2)

## Rules

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mau-Mau_(card_game)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Rules")]

The game is typically played with a 32-card pack, either a [French-suited pack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French-suited_pack "French-suited pack") from which the Twos, Threes, Fours, Fives and Sixes have been removed or, especially in Europe, with a 32-card [German pack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_pack "German pack"). For more than five players, two packs of cards may be used.

The aim is to be first to get rid of all of one's cards. Most of the time, the winner will have to say something at this point, usually "Mau". If the winner fails to say this, they do not win and instead must take penalty cards. If a player's last card is a Jack, they must reply differently, usually saying "Mau Mau".

Before the start of the game, a player who is not the dealer cuts the deck four times. If the player cuts 1–3 significant cards, they’re allowed to keep them if they want. However, if four cards where the cards are cut are found to be power cards, the deck needs to be reshuffled and the cut is repeated.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Mau_(card_game)#cite_note-:1-3) The players are each dealt a hand of cards (usually 5 or 6).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Mau_(card_game)#cite_note-:1-3) The rest is placed face down as the [stock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_(cards) "Stock (cards)") or stack. At the beginning of the game the topmost card is revealed and placed face up on the table then the players take it in turns to play their cards.

A card can only be played if it corresponds to the suit or value of the face-up card. For example, if it is the 10 of spades, only another spade or another 10 can be played (but see below for Jacks). If a player is not able to do this, they draw one card from the stack; If they can play this card, they may do so; otherwise, they keep the drawn card and their turn ends. When the drawing stack is empty, the playing stack (except for the topmost card) is shuffled and turned over to serve as a new drawing stack.

The 7, 8, Jack, and Ace of all suits are significant cards:

*   If a 7 is played, the next player has to draw two cards but may play. (A variant of the game allows the player facing the 7 to play another 7, in which case the player to their left must take 4 cards from the pack, unless they play a 7 too, in which case the player to their left must take 6 cards from the pack, unless they also play a 7, in which case the player to their left must take 8 cards from the pack.)
*   Any 8 forces the next player to miss their turn. (A variant of the game allows the player facing the 8 to play another 8, in which case the next player after them must play another 8 or miss a turn, etc.)
*   A Jack of any suit is the equivalent of a Joker and can be played on any card. The player who plays it then chooses a card suit. The next player then plays as if the Jack was of the chosen suit. (A variant of the game forbids Jacks from being placed on top of other Jacks)
*   If an Ace is played, one other card _must_ be played with it. If the player does not have another card, or cannot follow in suit or number, then the player must take a card from the pack. If a player's final card is an Ace, they cannot win on that turn.
*   When a player has only one card left, they must say "Mau" (even if it is an Ace); if that card is a Jack, they must say "Mau-Mau". Failure means that the player must take a card.
*   If the game is scored, _and_ the winning card is a Jack, then all points against the losers are doubled.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Mau_(card_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTEParlett2008447-4)

## Variants

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mau-Mau_(card_game)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Variants")]

### Austria and Bavaria

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mau-Mau_(card_game)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Austria and Bavaria")]

In [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria") and [Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavaria "Bavaria"), a variation is the 32-card game known as **Neuner** ("Nines"); in this variation, a Joker is added and the Nines are used as [wild cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_card_(playing_card) "Wild card (playing card)").[[4]](

**[Crazy Eights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_Eights "Crazy Eights")** is a card game for two to seven players.

**Crazy Eights** may also refer to:

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Museum of play located in Rochester, New York

This article is about the museum. For people nicknamed "the Strong", see [List of people known as the Strong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_known_as_the_Strong "List of people known as the Strong").

The Strong[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/9/90/Strong_museum_logo_-_Sep_2010.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Strong_museum_logo_-_Sep_2010.jpg)
[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Museum_of_Play_at_night.jpg/250px-Museum_of_Play_at_night.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Museum_of_Play_at_night.jpg)
Formation 1968;58 years ago(1968)
Founder[Margaret Strong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Woodbury_Strong "Margaret Woodbury Strong")
Type[Non-profit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonprofit_organization "Nonprofit organization")
Location[Rochester, NY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochester,_New_York "Rochester, New York"), [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")
Region served United States

**The Strong** is an interactive, collections-based [educational institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Educational_institution "Educational institution") in [Rochester, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochester,_New_York "Rochester, New York"), United States, devoted to the study and exploration of play.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Strong#cite_note-1) It carries out this mission through six programmatic arms called "Play Partners":

*   [The National Museum of Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Strong_National_Museum_of_Play "The Strong National Museum of Play")
*   [National Toy Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Toy_Hall_of_Fame "National Toy Hall of Fame")
*   [World Video Game Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Video_Game_Hall_of_Fame "World Video Game Hall of Fame")
*   [International Center for the History of Electronic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Center_for_the_History_of_Electronic_Games "International Center for the History of Electronic Games")
*   The Brian Sutton-Smith Library and Archives of Play
*   _[American Journal of Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Journal\_of\_Play "American Journal of Play")_
*   The Woodbury School

Independent and not-for-profit, The Strong houses hundreds of thousands of historical materials related to [play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play_(activity) "Play (activity)"). These enable a multifaceted array of research, exhibition, and other interpretive activities that serve a diverse audience of adults, families, children, students, teachers, scholars, collectors, and others around the globe.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Strong&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Strong was founded by [Margaret Woodbury Strong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Woodbury_Strong "Margaret Woodbury Strong") in 1968 as the "Margaret Woodbury Strong Museum of Fascination."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Strong#cite_note-history-2) On her death the next year, the museum inherited her estate and collection of dolls, toys, and other everyday objects. It moved to a new building in downtown Rochester in 1982.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Strong#cite_note-history-2) Market research in the 1990s led it to pivot toward more family-oriented programming, and in 2002 it acquired the [National Toy Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Toy_Hall_of_Fame "National Toy Hall of Fame"), which it renamed the Strong National Museum of Play on 2006.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Strong#cite_note-history-2) The institution rebranded itself The Strong in 2010, housing [The National Museum of Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_Museum_of_Play "The National Museum of Play") and four additional Play Partners.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Strong#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Strong#cite_note-4)

The Strong collects and preserves [artifacts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artifact_(archaeology) "Artifact (archaeology)"), [documents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Documents "Documents"), and other materials that illuminate the meaning and importance of play. The hundreds of thousands of objects in The Strong’s collections comprise the world’s most comprehensive assemblage of [toys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toys "Toys"), [games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game "Game"), [dolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doll "Doll"), [electronic games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_games "Electronic games"), and other items related to play, many of which are on display in approximately 100,000 square feet (26,200m2) of exhibition space.

[![Image 8: Map](https://maps.wikimedia.org/img/osm-intl,13,a,a,250x200.png?lang=en&domain=en.wikipedia.org&title=The_Strong_National_Museum_of_Play&revid=1363430780&groups=_474eb7c6d172f002f8b3d384db8b0f0f38f8a039&parser=parsoid) [Wikimedia](https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Maps_Terms_of_Use) | © [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#/map/0 "Show in full screen")
Established 1969;57 years ago(1969)
Location[Rochester, NY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochester,_New_York "Rochester, New York"), [USA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")
Type[Children's museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_museum "Children's museum")
Collections[Toys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toy "Toy"), [video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game "Video game")

Website[museumofplay.org](https://www.museumofplay.org/)

**The Strong National Museum of Play** (also known as just **The Strong Museum** or simply **the Strong**) is part of [The Strong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Strong "The Strong") in [Rochester, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochester,_New_York "Rochester, New York"), [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). Established in 1969 and initially based on the personal collection of Rochester native [Margaret Woodbury Strong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Woodbury_Strong "Margaret Woodbury Strong"), the museum opened to the public in 1982, after several years of planning, cataloguing, and exhibition development for the museum's new building in downtown Rochester.

For at least fifteen years after it opened, the mission of the museum was to interpret the social and cultural history of average Americans between 1830 and 1940, under the direction of H.J. Swinney and William T. Alderson. Mrs. Strong's collections of dolls and toys, American and European decorative arts, prints, paintings, Japanese crafts, and advertising ephemera provided a firm foundation for this mission, and were supplemented with collections purchased and donated to more fully support the museum's early mission. The museum received considerable local and national publicity/support as well as substantial financial support from the National Endowment for the Humanities' Exhibitions and Public Programs division.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#cite_note-1)

In the 1990s, the museum's Board of Trustees and director changed the museum's mission to collecting, preserving, and interpreting the history of play. Since then, it has refined and increased its collections (hundreds of thousands of items), and expanded thrice, in 1997, 2006, and 2023.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#cite_note-ctm-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#cite_note-Greenwood-4)

The museum is now one of six Play Partners of The Strong, which is also home to the [National Toy Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Toy_Hall_of_Fame "National Toy Hall of Fame"), the [International Center for the History of Electronic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Center_for_the_History_of_Electronic_Games "International Center for the History of Electronic Games"), the [World Video Game Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Video_Game_Hall_of_Fame "World Video Game Hall of Fame"), and the Brian Sutton-Smith Library and Archives of Play, and produces the _[American Journal of Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Journal\_of\_Play "American Journal of Play")_.

## About

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Strong_National_Museum_of_Play&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: About")]

Originally known as the "Margaret Woodbury Strong Museum" and later simply as the "Strong Museum", it became the "Strong National Museum of Play" in 2006, after completing renovations and an expansion that nearly doubled its size to 282,000 square feet (26,200 m 2).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#cite_note-ctm-3)

The National Museum of Play is the only collections-based museum anywhere devoted solely to the study of play, and although it is a history museum, it has the interactive characteristics of a [children's museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_museum "Children's museum"), making it the second largest museum of that type in the United States.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#cite_note-8) The museum includes exhibits that interpret the key elements of play, as well as allow guests to explore the worlds of [Sesame Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesame_Street "Sesame Street"), The [Berenstain Bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berenstain_Bears "Berenstain Bears"), Reading Adventureland, and the _Dancing Wings Butterfly Garden_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#cite_note-12)

### Exhibits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Strong_National_Museum_of_Play&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Exhibits")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Strong_Museum_1.jpg/330px-Strong_Museum_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Strong_Museum_1.jpg)

One area of the museum

The museum's exhibits are immersively themed to video games, storybooks, television shows, education, nature, history, comic books, carousel and train rides, and children's lifestyles. eGameRevolution is the first permanent video game exhibit in the US and includes the [World Video Game Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Video_Game_Hall_of_Fame "World Video Game Hall of Fame"). The [National Toy Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Toy_Hall_of_Fame "National Toy Hall of Fame") is at the museum. Dancing Wings Butterfly Garden features thousands of [butterflies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butterfly "Butterfly"), and is the largest indoor [butterfly garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butterfly_house "Butterfly house") in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"). [The Berenstain Bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berenstain_Bears "Berenstain Bears"): Down a Sunny Dirt Road is an original, permanent exhibit produced in partnership with the [Berenstain family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_and_Jan_Berenstain "Stan and Jan Berenstain").

In 2019, The Strong Museum received a US$700,000 grant from the [National Endowment for the Humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Endowment_for_the_Humanities "National Endowment for the Humanities") to develop an interactive exhibit space to show the influence of video games on culture, with plans to open in 2022.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#cite_note-13) After delays, the expansions were unveiled in July 2023, which included the ESL Digital Worlds exhibit, a new space to house the [World Video Game Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Video_Game_Hall_of_Fame "World Video Game Hall of Fame"), and the [Hasbro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasbro "Hasbro") Game Park, a large [board game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_game "Board game")-themed outdoor space. The additions added 90,000 square feet (8,400 m 2) of space at a final cost of US$75,000,000.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_National_Museum_of_Play#cite_note-Greenwood-4)

**Uno** ([/ˈ uː n oʊ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/2/24/LL-Q1860_%28eng%29-Flame%2C_not_lame-Uno_%28card_game%29.wav/LL-Q1860_%28eng%29-Flame%2C_not_lame-Uno_%28card_game%29.wav.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LL-Q1860_(eng)-Flame,_not_lame-Uno_(card_game).wav "File:LL-Q1860 (eng)-Flame, not lame-Uno (card game).wav"); from [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language") and [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language") for 'one'), stylized in [all caps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_caps "All caps") as **UNO**, is a proprietary American [shedding-type card game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Card_game#Shedding_games "Card game") originally developed in 1971 by [Merle Robbins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Robbins "Merle Robbins") in [Reading, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading,_Ohio "Reading, Ohio"), a [suburb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suburb "Suburb") of [Cincinnati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati "Cincinnati"), that housed International Inc., a gaming company acquired by [Mattel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattel "Mattel") on January 23, 1992.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-2)

The game is played with a [dedicated deck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedicated_deck_card_game "Dedicated deck card game") derived from the [crazy eights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_eights "Crazy eights") family of card games which, in turn, is based on the traditional German game of [mau-mau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau-Mau_(card_game) "Mau-Mau (card game)").

## History

The game was originally developed in 1971 by [Merle Robbins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merle_Robbins "Merle Robbins") in [Reading, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reading,_Ohio "Reading, Ohio"), a suburb of [Cincinnati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati "Cincinnati"). When his family and friends began to play more and more, he and his family mortgaged their home to raise $8,000 to have 5,000 copies of the game made.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-3) He sold it from his [barbershop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barber "Barber") at first, and local businesses began to sell it as well. Robbins later sold the rights to Uno to a group of friends headed by Robert Tezak, a funeral parlor owner in [Joliet, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joliet,_Illinois "Joliet, Illinois"), for $50,000 plus royalties of 10 cents per game. Tezak formed International Games, Inc., to market Uno, with offices behind his funeral parlor. The games were produced by Lewis Saltzman of Saltzman Printers in [Maywood, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maywood,_Illinois "Maywood, Illinois").

In 1992, International Games became part of the [Mattel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattel "Mattel") family of companies.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-instructions2001-4)

In 2018, Uno was inducted into the [National Toy Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Toy_Hall_of_Fame "National Toy Hall of Fame") alongside [pinball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinball "Pinball") and the [Magic 8 Ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_8_Ball "Magic 8 Ball").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-5) The [Strong National Museum of Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Strong_National_Museum_of_Play "The Strong National Museum of Play") also recognized the game for its fast pacing, wide age appeal, and enduring cultural impact as a staple of family entertainment.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-6)

In 2021, to celebrate the game's 50th anniversary, [Mattel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattel "Mattel") hosted the inaugural Uno Championship Series.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-7) The invitational tournament culminated in a grand finale at the [HyperX Esports Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HyperX_Arena "HyperX Arena") in [Las Vegas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Vegas "Las Vegas") on November 11, 2021, where the first official Uno World Champion was crowned and awarded a $50,000 grand prize.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-8)

## Official rules

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Uno.jpg/250px-Uno.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Uno.jpg)

Uno cards

The aim of the game is to be the first player to play all of one's own cards.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-:1-9) Prior to the 2022 rule changes, the official objective was to be the first player to score 500 points. This was achieved across multiple rounds; players scored points by being the first to play all their cards and received points for the cards still held by the other players. This format remains an optional way to play.

Uno includes 108 cards: 25 in each of four color suits (red, yellow, green, blue), each suit consisting of one zero, two each of 1 through 9, and two each of the action cards "Skip", "Draw Two", and "Reverse". The deck also contains four "Wild" cards and four "Wild Draw Four".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-UNO-10) Sets manufactured since 2015 include 112 cards, adding one "Wild Swap Hands" (2015–17) or "Wild Shuffle Hands" (since 2017) Wild Card and three customizable Wild cards.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-mattelinst-1)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/UNO_cards_deck.svg/250px-UNO_cards_deck.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UNO_cards_deck.svg)

Uno cards deck

For each hand, a dealer is determined by having each player randomly draw one card from the deck. The player with the highest number card deals, and all cards are reshuffled into the deck to begin the dealing.

To start a hand, seven cards are dealt to each player, and the top card of the remaining deck is flipped over and set aside to begin the discard pile. The player to the dealer's left plays first unless the first card on the discard pile is an action or Wild card (see below). On a player's turn, they must do one of the following:

*   play one card matching the discard in color, number, or symbol
*   play a Wild card or a Wild Draw Four card if allowed to (see restrictions below)
*   draw the top card from the deck and optionally play it if possible

Cards are played by laying them face-up on top of the discard pile. Play initially proceeds clockwise around the table.

Action or Wild cards have the following effects:

| Card | Effect when played from hand | Effect as first discard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Skip | Next player in sequence misses a turn | Player to dealer's left misses a turn |
| Reverse | Order of play switches directions (clockwise to counterclockwise, or vice versa) | Dealer plays first; play proceeds counterclockwise |
| Draw Two (+2) | Next player in sequence draws two cards and misses a turn | Player to dealer's left draws two cards and misses a turn |
| Wild | Player declares the next color to be matched (may be used on any turn even if the player has any card of matching color) | Player to dealer's left declares the first color to be matched and takes the first turn |
| Wild Draw Four | Player declares the next color to be matched; next player in sequence draws four cards and misses a turn. May be legally played if the player has no cards of the current color (see [Penalties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#Penalties)) | Card is returned to the deck, then a new card is laid down into the discard pile (deck may be reshuffled first if needed) |

*   A player who draws a card from the deck must choose whether to play that card immediately or keep it. No cards already in their hand may be played on that turn.
*   A Wild card may be played on any turn, even if the player holding it has cards that will match the current color, number, and/or symbol.
*   A Wild Draw Four card may be played only if the player holding it has no cards matching the current color. The player may have cards of a different color matching the current number/symbol or a Wild card and still play the Wild Draw Four card.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-UNO-10) A player who plays a Wild Draw Four may be challenged by the next player in sequence (see [Penalties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#Penalties)) to prove that their hand meets this condition. An illegally played Wild Draw Four card incurs no penalty for its user unless challenged.
*   A player using a Wild or Wild Draw Four card must declare the new matching color before ending their turn, and may declare the current color if desired.
*   If the draw deck runs out during play, the discard pile is shuffled to create a new deck. Play then proceeds normally.
*   It is illegal to trade cards of any sort with any other player at any time.

A player who plays their penultimate card must indicate it to the other players by calling out "Uno".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-11)

The first player to get rid of their last card ("going out") wins the hand and scores points for the cards held by each other player. Number cards count their face value, all action cards count 20, and Wild and Wild Draw Four cards count 50. If a Draw Two or Wild Draw Four card is played to go out, the next player in the sequence must draw the appropriate number of cards before the score is tallied.

The first player to score 500 points wins the game.

### Penalties

*   If a player does not call "Uno" while laying down their penultimate card and is caught before the next player in sequence takes their turn (i.e., plays a card from their hand, draws from the deck, or touches the discard pile), they must draw two cards as a penalty. If the player is not caught in time or remembers to call "Uno" before being caught, no penalty applies to that player.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-UNO-10)
*   If a player plays a Wild Draw Four card, the next player in turn order may choose to challenge its use. The player who used the Wild Draw Four must privately show their hand to the challenging player in order to demonstrate that they had no cards of prior matching color. If the challenge is successful, the challenged player must draw four cards instead and play continues with the challenger. Otherwise, the challenger must draw six cards – the four cards they were already required to draw plus two more cards – and miss their turn.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-UNO-10) In either case, the Wild Draw Four stays with its chosen color.

### Two-player game

In a two-player game, the Reverse card acts like a Skip card; when played, the other player misses a turn.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-12) This rule is not mentioned in the instruction sheets of modern copies of the game.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-:1-9)

### House rules

The following house rules are suggested in some official Uno instruction sets to alter the game:

*   **Progressive or Stacking Uno**: If a draw card is played, and the next player in turn order has a card with the same symbol, that player can play that card and "stack" the penalty, which adds to the current penalty and passes it to the next player[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-UNO-10) (although a +4 cannot be stacked on a +2, or vice versa).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-dex-13) This house rule is so commonly used that there was widespread Twitter surprise in 2019 when [Mattel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattel "Mattel") stated that stacking was not part of the standard rules of Uno.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-dex-13) They explicitly clarified that players cannot stack Draw Two (+2) or Wild Draw Four (+4) cards, confirming that stacking is strictly a house rule.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-14)
*   **Seven-O**: Every time a "7" is played, whoever played it must swap hands with another player of their choice before ending their turn. Every time a "0" is played, all players pass their hands to the next player in the current direction of play, after which play continues normally.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-UNO-10)
*   **Jump-In**: If a player has exactly the same card (both number and color) as the top card of the discard pile, they may play it immediately, even if it is not their turn. Play then continues as if that player had just taken their turn.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-UNO-10)

### 2015 rule changes

The two new types of Wild cards have the following functions:

*   **Wild Swap Hands**: The player using this card chooses another player with whom they swap cards in their respective hands.
*   **Wild Customizable**: There are three copies of this; these cards are blank and can have a house rule assigned to them.

Each of these cards can be played on any turn and is worth 40 points when a player goes out.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-Uno_2015-15)

### 2017 rule changes

Wild Swap Hands was replaced in 2017 by **Wild Shuffle Hands**; the player using this new card collects all cards held by all players, then shuffles and re-deals them, starting from the player to their left. This card can also be played on any turn and is also worth 40 points when a player goes out.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-mattelinst-1)

### 2022 rule changes

The goal to reach a certain number of points has been demoted and replaced with the one commonly used by most players, which is to be the first player to go out. If played for points, each Wild card is worth 50 points regardless of type. There is no longer an official method to determine the dealer. In addition, if the first card flipped at the start of a game is an Action or Wild card, it is ignored and another card is flipped until a number card comes up.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-:1-9)

## Card and deck styles

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Uno_Old_Deck.jpg/250px-Uno_Old_Deck.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Uno_Old_Deck.jpg)

A deck of English Uno cards from 1994. This particular deck uses the older card design, where letters appear on the action cards instead of symbols.

Modern Uno action cards bear symbols which denote their action, except for the Wild cards which still bear the word "Wild". Before the design change, such cards in English versions of the game had letters only. Earlier English versions can be recognized by the absence of the white rim that surrounds the edge of most Uno cards.

Other versions of the game use symbols and images in both old and new designs, especially ones with Wild cards that do not bear the word "Wild". There are also language-free versions of the newer styles that do not bear the word "Wild" but have the same styling.

The 2010 "Uno Mod" edition uses symbols instead of letters or numbers.

On September 16, 2017, Mattel released Uno ColorAdd, which was designed specifically for [colorblind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_blindness "Color blindness") people.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-colorblind-16)

On October 1, 2019, Mattel released a [Braille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braille "Braille") version of their game with Mark Riccobono, president of the [National Federation of the Blind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Federation_of_the_Blind "National Federation of the Blind"). Riccobono said in a press release, "The fact that a blind person is now able to play a classic game of UNO straight out of the box with both blind and sighted friends or family members is a truly meaningful moment for our community."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-braille_1-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-18)

The year 2024 saw the introduction of small shapes into the decks for better color blindness accessibility, part of a larger effort by Mattel to make 80% of its game catalog more playable to people in that disability sector.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-Uno_Color_Shapes-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-20) The shapes used are [diamonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lozenge_(shape) "Lozenge (shape)") for yellow, circles for red, squares for blue, and triangles for green.

### Uno H2O

**Uno H 2 O** differs from the standard game in that the cards are transparent and waterproof. Play is identical to the standard pre-2015 Uno game, with the addition of two types of "Wild Downpour" cards. When one of these is played, all other players must draw either one or two cards as indicated on the card. The player using it may then declare the next color to be matched. Several of the other sets have been released in this format.

### _Uno Fandom_ series

In 2023, Mattel's imprint Mattel Creations released a special collector's series of Uno games based on fandom of fictional properties and sports teams. The initial group of sets in this series included those based on all 32 [NFL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL "NFL") teams and several fictional properties, including _[Star Trek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star\_Trek "Star Trek")_, _[Harry Potter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry\_Potter "Harry Potter")_, _[Masters of the Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masters\_of\_the\_Universe "Masters of the Universe")_, _[Avatar: the Last Airbender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avatar:\_the\_Last\_Airbender "Avatar: the Last Airbender")_ and _[Monster High](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monster\_High "Monster High")_. ## Variations

Many variations from standard gameplay exist, such as Elimination Uno, Speed Uno and Pirate Uno.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-29)

On February 13, 2018, Mattel released a spin-off of Uno entitled _**Dos**_; the game is differentiated primarily by having a "center row" of discard piles, where pairs of cards that add up to the sum of a card on the top of one of the piles may be discarded.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-32)

The game can be played with two decks of standard playing cards if the [jokers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joker_(playing_card) "Joker (playing card)") are marked up as the zeroes of the four suits and the royalty treated as the special cards.

After mixed reviews for the original game, Mattel released another version of Dos titled _**Dos Second Edition**_,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-33) which plays more like Uno but still includes some rules from the original Dos.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-34) The new Dos has Skip, Reverse and Draw Two cards (which were not included in the original Dos) but retains the Wild Dos Card and the two discard piles. A new card was introduced known as the Wild Play Two Card, forcing the next player to play a minimum of two cards, if they can not they play nothing and draw two cards. Like Uno, players start with seven cards and the main way to win is by discarding all cards first.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-35)

## Spin-offs

### Slot machines

In 2002, [International Gaming Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Game_Technology_(1975%E2%80%932015) "International Game Technology (1975–2015)") introduced a "pod concept" for grouping the prize winnings of similarly themed and newly released MegaJackpot games into one collective pool.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-36) Among these was the new Famous Games pod, unveiling two new Mattel-licensed machines, UNO Slots and Magic 8 Ball slots. In the following two years, additional properties were tied into the pod, along with the Video Slot versions of both UNO and Magic 8 Ball.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-:0-37)

The UNO slot machine featured a basic vertical 3 wheel system, along with 3 additional horizontal wheels that would activate when 3 UNO bonus symbols in any position were landed with the maximum bet wagered.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-38) Meanwhile, the UNO Video Slot Machine featured a 5 reel, 15 line Video system with additional UNO Attack and UNO Triple bonus games awarded based on the symbols landed.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-39) Both versions saw limited releases to various Native American gaming centers.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-:0-37)

### Uno: The Game Show

In March 2013, it was announced that [Mattel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattel "Mattel") and the Gurin Company[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-41) were teaming up to create a game show based on the card game, produced as a half-hour daily strip with a $100,000 cash jackpot along with a primetime version in which contestants competed for $1 million. However, the idea was scrapped later on.

On February 4, 2021, an action heist comedy film based on the game was announced to be in development for [Mattel Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattel_Films "Mattel Films") with [Lil Yachty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Yachty "Lil Yachty") of record label [Quality Control Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quality_Control_Music "Quality Control Music") developing and being eyed for the lead role alongside the label's managers Kevin "Coach K" Lee and Pierre "P" Thomas, and Brian Sher for Quality Films producing, Marcy Kelly writing, and Robbie Brenner and Kevin McKeon leading the project as executive producer and supervising producer, respectively.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-42)

## Complexity

Uno has been studied from the perspective of [combinatorial game theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combinatorial_game_theory "Combinatorial game theory"). When played by two uncooperative players, Uno has been shown to be [solvable in polynomial time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P_(complexity) "P (complexity)"). For two players playing cooperatively, the game becomes [NP-complete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NP-complete "NP-complete").

A [solitaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solitaire "Solitaire") variant of the game where a player inspects their hand and decides if there is an order in which every card can be played has been shown to be solvable in polynomial time for a constant number of colours and numbers (as in the standard Uno deck). For the general case with many colors and many numbers, the problem is NP-complete.

The problem of finding a way to play all cards in a hand is equivalent to searching for a [Hamiltonian path](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiltonian_path "Hamiltonian path") on a graph with vertices representing each card, and edges connecting cards that share a colour or number.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-43)

## Reception

The _[Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Games\_(magazine) "Games (magazine)")_ magazine included _Uno_ in their "Top 100 Games of 1980", noting that the game "borrows so much from the familiar card game of Crazy Eights" but that "it's a much better game and just as simple to learn".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-44) They would later include the game in their "Top 100 Games of 1982", noting that its "popularity is based on its simplicity, not on its strategic aspects" and that "the game has a rummylike scoring system".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uno_(card_game)#cite_note-45)

Amazing America's Kevin Kotwas shares the hidden history of Uno, now the most popular card game in the world.

**David Parlett** (born 18 May 1939 in London)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-1) is a games scholar, historian,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-2) and translator from South London, who has studied both [card games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Card_game "Card game")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-3) and [board games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_game "Board game").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-5) He is the president of the [British Skat Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Skat_Association "British Skat Association").

## Life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_Parlett&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

David Sidney Parlett was born in London on 18 May 1939 to Sidney Thomas Parlett and Eleanor May Parlett, née Nunan. He is one of three brothers. During the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Parlett lived in [Barry, Glamorgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry,_Vale_of_Glamorgan "Barry, Vale of Glamorgan"). He was educated at [Battersea Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battersea_Grammar_School "Battersea Grammar School") and the [University College of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth_University "Aberystwyth University") in [Aberystwyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth "Aberystwyth"). He has a BA in Modern Languages. Parlett was a technical writer with PR companies and later a freelance writer for _Games & Puzzles_ magazine. He is married to Barbara and they have a son and a daughter.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-6)

## Works

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=David_Parlett&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Works")]

His published works include many popular books on games such as _Penguin Book of Card Games_,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-7) as well as the more academic volumes _The Oxford Guide to Card Games_ and _The Oxford History of Board Games_,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-8) both now out of print. Parlett has also invented many card games and board games. The most successful of these is _[Hare and Tortoise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hare\_and\_Tortoise "Hare and Tortoise")_ (1974). Its German edition was awarded [Spiel des Jahres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiel_des_Jahres "Spiel des Jahres") (Game of the Year) in 1979.

Parlett is a [Quaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers "Quakers").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parlett#cite_note-9)

An Inormation System (IS) is “an arrangement o people, data,

processes and inormation technology that interact to collect, pro-

According to Bunge

[[9](https://www.scribd.com/document/686523308/Games-as-Information-Systems-SBSI-2021)]

as well as between those components and the environment”. In his defnition, the elements o the systems need to act on each

the action o one element on the other, in which case one is the agent and the other is the patient, and the interactio n, in which

there are reciprocal actions[[9](https://www.scribd.com/document/686523308/Games-as-Information-Systems-SBSI-2021)].

parts”. The system has new properties that emerge rom the actions and interactions between the parts and that do not exist in the parts

The DOI Foundation is a not-for-profit organization. We govern the Digital Object Identifier (DOI) system on behalf of the agencies who manage DOI registries and provide services to their respective communities. We are the registration authority for the ISO standard (ISO 26324) for the DOI system and we are governed by our Registration Agencies.

Read more about us, our operations and our community of communities from construction to entertainment to scholarly research.

[learn more](https://www.doi.org/the-foundation/about-us/)

![Image 2](https://www.doi.org/images/globe.svg)

## WHO IS THE DOI FOUNDATION COMMUNITY?

We are an international community of communities bound by a common interest in persistent infrastructure. So far, we have welcomed agencies that manage communities spanning entertainment, standards, the built environment, natural history collections, scholarly communications, and research data.

Read more about our Registration Agencies and what they offer

[learn more](https://www.doi.org/the-community/what-are-registration-agencies/)

![Image 3](https://www.doi.org/images/target.svg)

## WHAT IS THE DIGITAL OBJECT IDENTIFIER (DOI)?

A DOI name is a digital identifier of an object, any object — physical, digital, or abstract. DOIs solve a common problem: keeping track of things. Things can be matter, material, content, or activities.

Designed to be used by humans as well as machines, DOIs identify objects persistently. They allow things to be uniquely identified and accessed reliably. You know what you have, where it is, and others can track it too.

Read more about the identifier, its benefits, and how it’s used

[learn more](https://www.doi.org/the-identifier/what-is-a-doi/)

![Image 4](https://www.doi.org/images/board/jclark.jpg)

## Jonathan Clark

It is with great sadness that we share that Jonathan Clark died suddenly on August 11, 2026. Jonathan had been the Managing Agent of the DOI Foundation since 2015. Over those years, he guided the DOI Foundation with a steady hand and was a generous colleague to many across our community.   
  
 Our thoughts are with his family, friends, and the many individuals and organizations he worked alongside. We will share a fuller tribute to Jonathan soon.   
  
 The DOI system and services continue to operate normally under the direction of the DOI Foundation Board.

## Try resolving a DOI name

Type or paste a known DOI name exactly—including its prefix and suffix—into the text box below and then ‘submit’ to resolve it.

DOIs include a prefix (prefixes always start with `10.`) and a suffix, separated by a forward slash (`/`). Prefacing the DOI with `doi.org/` will turn it into an actionable link, for example, [https://doi.org/10.5334/dsj-2017-040](https://doi.org/10.5334/dsj-2017-040). Clicking that link will ‘resolve’ it, i.e. redirect to the latest information about the object it identifies, even if the object changes or moves.

# Play Lab

![Image 7: Play Lab exterior](https://www.museumofplay.org/app/uploads/2022/03/Play-Lab-exterior-1024x498.jpg)

Invent, construct, and create in The Strong’s 800-square-foot _Play Lab_ on the museum’s first floor (near the _Field of Play_ exhibit). Unlock the educational power of play and enter a playful maker space with daily programming based around monthly themes.

Every month be introduced to a new topic of inquiry such as printmaking, sound, and circuitry. Gain scaffolding assistance from museum staff and guest creators. Experiment with related tools and equipment such as looms, saws, and Oculus. Take time to create, engage with others, and reflect. Additional programs focus on game and toy development, LEGO bricks, sound, printmaking, messy play, painting, and more.

To learn more, see Play Lab [Frequently Asked Questions](https://www.museumofplay.org/exhibits/museum-exhibits/play-lab-faqs/).

![Image 8: Play Lab interior](https://www.museumofplay.org/app/uploads/2022/03/Play-Lab2-web-1024x498.jpg)

See the [Play Lab’s social story](https://www.museumofplay.org/visit/accessibility/visiting-the-play-lab/).

## About us

The DOI Foundation is a not-for-profit organization. We govern the Digital Object Identifier (DOI) system on behalf of the agencies who manage DOI registries and provide services to their respective communities. We are the registration authority for the ISO standard (ISO 26324) for the DOI system and we are governed by our Registration Agencies. Please direct all DOI ID questions & requests about registration status to the agency where registered - as this page does not respond to inquiries.

I blinked and [Crossref](https://www.linkedin.com/company/crossref?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text) hit 2 billion matched citation links! I know, "billion" is one of those numbers so big it stops meaning anything. So let me put it this way: this is 2,000,000,000 times some researchers pointed to other research and said: "I came from this, a bit." Tiny acts of acknowledgement, building on each other - papers to papers, data to papers, papers to code. The whole messy, beautiful graph of how knowledge actually travels. That's provenance and infrastructure at scale - and it's all open and yours to use. The blog's worth a read - [Kora Korzec](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/kora-korzec?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text), [Dominika Tkaczyk](https://ie.linkedin.com/in/dtkaczyk?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text), and [Jason Portenoy](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jason-portenoy?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text) explain it better than I just did! # Resources

## Factsheets

## DOI® Resolution Documentation

[< back to the Resources page](https://www.doi.org/the-identifier/resources/)

1. [Resolving DOIs Using the Proxy Server System](https://www.doi.org/the-identifier/resources/factsheets/doi-resolution-documentation#1-resolving-dois-using-the-proxy-server-system)  
 2. [Encoding DOIs for Use in URIs](https://www.doi.org/the-identifier/resources/factsheets/doi-resolution-documentation#2-encoding-dois-for-use-in-uris)  
 3. [Proxy Server Query Parameters](https://www.doi.org/the-identifier/resources/factsheets/doi-resolution-documentation#3-proxy-server-query-parameters)  
 4. [Which RA?](https://www.doi.org/the-identifier/resources/factsheets/doi-resolution-documentation#4-which-ra)  
 5. [Proxy Server REST API](https://www.doi.org/the-identifier/resources/factsheets/doi-resolution-documentation#5-proxy-server-rest-api)

_Note that this information, and additional information about the DOI Proxy Server System, Resolution and Numbering, can be found in the [DOI Handbook](https://www.doi.org/the-identifier/resources/handbook/)._

Users may resolve DOI names that are structured to use the DOI system Proxy Server (https://doi.org (preferred)). The resolution of the DOI name in this case depends on the use of URL syntax: the example DOI name doi:10.10.123/456 would be resolved from the address: “https://doi.org/10.123/456”. Any standard browser encountering a DOI name in this form will be able to resolve it. The proxy service (both doi.org and the earlier but no longer preferred dx.doi.org) is accessible over IPv6, and supports DNSSEC. The proxy servers respond to HTTPS (preferred) as well as HTTP requests.

### 1. Resolving DOIs using the Proxy Server System

The DOI system uses the Handle System® to manage digital objects (see the DOI Factsheet “[DOI System and the Handle System](https://www.doi.org/the-identifier/resources/factsheets/doi-system-and-the-handle-system)”). At the infrastructure level, DOI names are handles.

The DOI system Proxy Server is basically a web server that knows how to talk to the Handle System, and at this writing, most DOI® names found on the web are embedded in URLs that use the proxy server for DOI name resolution. For any HTTP request that combines the proxy’s domain name with a DOI name, for example

[https://doi.org/10.1000/demo_DOI](https://doi.org/10.1000/demo_DOI)

the proxy will query the Handle System for the DOI name, take the URL in the handle record (or if there are multiple URLs in the handle record it will select one, and that selection is in no particular order) and send an HTTP redirect to that URL to the user’s web browser.

Increasing numbers of DOI names include data in addition to the single default URL. This is sometimes referenced as multiple resolution. These added values are intended for use by more advanced applications which have the ability to take advantage of multiple pieces of data, e.g., the location of enhanced metadata or related documents.

In addition to handle values of type URL, the proxy server understands values of handle value type 10320/loc. These values contain XML describing multiple redirection endpoints for the DOI name and conditions under which the proxy should use them. For further documentation see _DOI Handbook_ Section 3.8.4.3, [Resolution of Multiple URLs using the 10320/loc Handle Type](https://www.doi.org/the-identifier/resources/handbook/3_resolution/#3.8.4.3).

The proxy server is configured to display a “DOI Name Not Found” error page when queried for a DOI name that it cannot find.

The DOI names 10.1000/demo_DOI and 10.1000/demo_DOI/ are both valid DOI names, but it is unlikely that a DOI name will be created with a trailing slash. If a resolution request for a DOI name with a trailing slash is received by the proxy server and that DOI name is not found, the proxy server will return an error report that includes a warning that the requested DOI name contained a trailing slash, and a link to click to resolve the same string without the slash.

The DOI system Proxy Server is really multiple servers running at multiple locations, with the load distributed evenly across all servers. To speed resolution, the proxy servers cache handle values, with the TTL set to 24 hours. This means that if a handle value is changed, it can take up to 24 hours before the new value is returned.

Note that the IDF also runs a proxy server for the [shortDOI™ Service](http://shortdoi.org/) that is not part of this DOI system Proxy Server specification.

### 2. Encoding DOIs for use in URIs

The Handle System uses UTF-8, a Unicode implementation, and has no character set constraints. But the DOI system Proxy Server is a web server that sends redirects to web browsers using HTTP syntax, so characters in DOI names that may not be interpreted correctly by web browsers, for example ‘?’, should be avoided or encoded. A non-ASCII character in a DOI name should be converted to UTF-8, and each UTF-8 byte that isn’t ASCII should be %encoded.

The “#” is another example. Only if you send the DOI system Proxy Server the DOI name

10.1000/res#test

encoded as

https://doi.org/10.1000/res%23test

will the proxy correctly resolve the DOI name. If it is not encoded, #test will be treated as a fragment and removed by the web browser before it gets to the proxy, which will then attempt to resolve 10.1000/res instead.

Tables 1 and 2 summarize the encoding guidelines for DOI. URLs have the most restricted set of characters. Table 1 lists the characters that should always be hex encoded. Table 2 lists additional characters where it is recommended that characters be replaced by hex-encoding. The distinction between the lists is between practical experience with current web browsers and the more formal specification of URL syntax. In the DOI Directory all characters represent themselves.

#### Table 1: Mandatory Encoding

| Character | Encoding |
| --- | --- |
| % | (%25) |
| " | (%22) |
| # | (%23) |
| SPACE | (%20) |
| ? | (%3F) |

#### Table 2: Recommended Encoding

| Character | Encoding |
| --- | --- |
| < | (%3C) |
| > | (%3E) |
| { | (%7B) |
| } | (%7D) |
| ^ | (%5E) |
| [ | (%5B) |
| ] | (%5D) |
| ` | (%60) |
| | | (%7C) |
| \ | (%5C) |
| + | (%2B) |

Note also that web browser treatment of “/./” and “/../” can be inconsistent. It is recommended that one of the slashes be percent encoded, e.g., change “/./” to “/.%2F” and “/../” to “/..%2F”.

### 3. Proxy Server query parameters

noredirect Do not redirect using URL or 10320/loc values; display handle values instead.ignore_aliases Ordinarily the proxy will take a handle value of type HS\_ALIAS to be a handle that should be resolved instead of the input handle; with this parameter values of type HS\_ALIAS are ignored.auth Authoritative query. The proxy will bypass its cache and resolve the handle at an authoritative server.cert Certified query. The proxy will require an authenticated response from the handle server. Not generally needed by end users.index Only resolve the handle value at the specified index. May be repeated to resolve multiple indices.type Only resolve handle values of the specified type. May be repeated to resolve multiple types.urlappend The value of this parameter is appended to the end of the URL used for redirection.locatt=key:value For multiple redirection; specifies a key:value pair to determine the choice of redirection from 10320/loc values.action=showurls For multiple redirection; returns an XML representation of the possible redirect locations.nols=y Some libraries and other institutions use a special cookie to cause the DOI system Proxy Server to redirect users to an “appropriate copy” using a local service. For example users may be redirected to the full text of a journal article already purchased by the library, instead of a landing page indicating a fee. Users can add the “nols=y” query parameter to prevent the local service redirect.
### 4. Which RA?

Which RA? is a simple service that has been built to examine the type/value pairs returned from handle resolution and provide specific information that is available from the doi.org Proxy System. This service returns the name of the DOI Registration Agency (RA) responsible for a specific DOI, or group of DOIs. When a DOI name is appended to the string “https://doi.org/doiRA/”, a resolution (HTTP GET) of that URL will return a bit of JSON specifying the name of the RA. Resolving [https://doi.org/doiRA/10.5240/B1FA-0EEC-C316-3316-3A73-L](https://doi.org/doiRA/10.5240/B1FA-0EEC-C316-3316-3A73-L) will return:

```
[  
  {  
    "DOI": "10.5240/B1FA-0EEC-C316-3316-3A73-L",  
    "RA": "EIDR"  
  }  
]
```

A full list of RA names and abbreviations can be found [here](https://www.doi.org/the-community/existing-registration-agencies/). Using commas in the URL string to delineate multiple DOIs will return multiple results in one request. Possible error states include “Invalid DOI”, “DOI does not exist” and “Unknown”.

### 5. Proxy Server REST API

The DOI system Proxy Server REST API allows programmatic access to DOI name resolution using HTTP.

#### Example Request/Response

A REST API request can be made by performing a standard HTTP GET of

`/api/handles/<handle>`

The API returns JSON.

For example, https://doi.org/api/handles/10.1000/1 yields the response

```
{
  "responseCode": 1,
  "handle": "10.1000/1",
  "values": [
	{
	  "index": 100,
	  "type": "HS_ADMIN",
	  "data": {
		"format": "admin",
		"value": {
		  "handle": "0.NA/10.1000",
		  "index": 200,
		  "permissions": "011111111111"
		}
	  },
	  "ttl": 86400,
	  "timestamp": "2000-04-13T15:08:57Z"
	},
	{
	  "index": 1,
	  "type": "URL",
	  "data": { "format": "string", "value": "http://www.doi.org/index.html" },
	  "ttl": 86400,
	  "timestamp": "2004-09-10T19:49:59Z"
	}
  ]
}
```

#### Response Format

The response is a JSON object which includes a “responseCode” (an integer referring to a Handle protocol response code), an echo of the “handle” resolved, and either a list of “values” or, in the case of an error, an optional “message” which is a string describing the error.

Each value is a JSON object with generally 5 attributes:

*   “index” : an integer
*   “type” : a string
*   “data” : an object, see below
*   “ttl” : the time-to-live in seconds of the value, an integer (or, in the rare case of an absolute expiration time, that expiration time as an ISO8601-formatted string)
*   “timestamp” : an ISO8601-formatted string

Handle value data is an object with properties “format”, a string, and “value”.

*   If “format”=“string”, “value” is a string, representing the data as a UTF-8 string.
*   If “format”=“base64”, “value” is a string, with a BASE64 encoding of the data.
*   If “format”=“hex”, “value” is a string, with a hex encoding of the data.
*   If “format”=“admin”, “value” is an object, representing an HS_ADMIN value, with properties “handle” (a string), “index” (an integer), and “permissions” (a string, representing the bitmask of permissions).

*   If “format”=“site”, “value” is an object, representing an HS_SITE value. As the structure of this object is complicated and generally of limited technical interest it is currently omitted from this documentation.

*   1 : Success. (HTTP 200 OK)
*   2 : Error. Something unexpected went wrong during handle resolution. (HTTP 500 Internal Server Error)
*   100 : Handle Not Found. (HTTP 404 Not Found)

The presence of the “pretty” query parameter instructs the server to pretty-print the JSON output.

The “auth” query parameter instructs the proxy server to bypass its cache and query a primary handle server directly for the newest handle data.

The “cert” query parameter instructs the proxy server to request an authenticated response from the source handle server. Not generally needed by end users.

The “type” and “index” query parameters allow the resolution response to be restricted to specific types and indexes of interest. Multiple “type” and “index” parameters are allowed and values are returned which match any of the specified types or indexes. For example,

# Block by Block: Leslie Scott’s Jenga Game (or, in Swahili, Zuia kwa kuzuia: Mchezo wa Jenga wa Leslie Scott)

[![Image 9: The original Jenga game, 1983. Leslie Scott Associates, The Strong, Rochester, New York.](https://www.museumofplay.org/app/uploads/2021/08/1081622.jpg)](https://www.museumofplay.org/sites/default/files/blog/full-images/108%2C1622.jpg "The original Jenga game, 1983. Leslie Scott Associates, The Strong, Rochester, New York.") Born in Tanganyika (now the Republic of Tanzania) in East Africa, English national Leslie Scott and her family moved to Ghana, a country rich in wood, when she was 18. She and her family had played a block stacking game since childhood, and she commissioned sets of blocks from a local sawmill. In her 20s, Scott moved to Oxford, England, and brought some block sets with her. Her British friends loved the game to obsession, she says, “but it took me a while to realize that it didn’t actually exist as a product.”

While it wasn’t exactly her eureka moment, it was at least a flash of inspiration, the kind many game inventors hope for and some achieve. But Jenga’s success didn’t happen overnight. Scott first commissioned 100 games built by Camphill, a community in Yorkshire for people with learning disabilities. According to Scott, “They agreed provided that, if the game was a success, I’d find an alternative manufacturer, as they didn’t want to be stuck making little blocks for the rest of their lives.” And she added, “Computer games were just taking off, and everyone thought the board game was dead.” The English department store Harrod’s agreed to order some sets of the game, if Scott would demonstrate them during the Christmas holidays. The game was selling, but she had mounting debts.

It was the North American—initially the Canadian—market that spurred greater interest in Jenga. After an Irwin Toys executive spotted the game being demonstrated at a Toronto department store, he brought it to Irwin, which signed a deal to produce it in Canada and brought the game to the 1986 Canada Toy Fair. And Irwin had connections with (and would eventually be purchased by) Hasbro, Inc. Both companies, however, thoroughly disliked the name Jenga.

[![Image 10: Leslie Scott and Jenga, 2020, photo by Sue Macpherson ARPS. The Strong, Rochester, New York.](https://www.museumofplay.org/app/uploads/2021/08/LeslielowL-resized.jpg)](https://www.museumofplay.org/sites/default/files/blog/full-images/LeslielowL%20(resized).jpg "Leslie Scott and Jenga, 2020, photo by Sue Macpherson ARPS. The Strong, Rochester, New York.")

Scott grew up speaking both English and Swahili, and “jenga” comes from the Swahili _kujenga_—to build. With a love of games and gaming—she’d once designed learning games for corporate development―she said, “I’d thought very hard about the name, though. I had deliberately not chosen a descriptive name like Tumbling Towers. I had this idea: that when you said Jenga, everyone would think of the game and nothing else.” The name was almost a deal-breaker for the industry giants, but her instincts were correct. We see unique or foreign language-derived names and brands everywhere. They purposefully call to mind only the products they represent. As Scott later said, “I stuck to my guns.”

Hasbro’s Hassenfeld brothers first saw and played Jenga, at Stephen Hassenfeld’s New York apartment, and his brother Alan later wrote that they “fell in love with it. When we launched in 1986, we were at the cusp of video games like ColecoVision and Atari. But one of the most magical things about Jenga was that you could open up the box and just start playing immediately. You can do a lot of market research, but every once in a while you look at a product and, in the bottom of your stomach, you just know it’s good.”

As a proprietary tabletop game, Jenga has been ranked second only to Monopoly in terms of worldwide sales, which is especially interesting considering how long Monopoly has been on the market. In terms of numbers, a recent estimate topped 80 million Jenga games sold. The game has proved fun for young and old and from two to multiple players. As Leslie Scott also told the _Oxford Times_, “In a world that was getting more and more complex, this was something simple, and sometimes simple works.” And that simplicity and universal appeal helped earn Jenga a place as one of the three 2020 inductees to the National Toy Hall of Fame.

September 16, 2026

The Strong’s National Toy Hall of Fame announces the 2026 National Toy Hall of Fame finalists.

[More Information](https://www.museumofplay.org/exhibits/toy-hall-of-fame/2026-finalists/)

![Image 9: 2026 World Video Game Hall of Fame Inductees](https://www.museumofplay.org/app/uploads/2026/05/WVGHOF-2026-SQ.jpg)

May 7, 2026

The Strong welcomes Angry Birds, Dragon Quest, EA Sports FIFA International Soccer, and Silent Hill to the 2026 World Video Game Hall of Fame.

[More Information](https://www.museumofplay.org/exhibits/world-video-game-hall-of-fame/inducted-games/)

![Image 10: 2026 Video Game Finalists](https://www.museumofplay.org/app/uploads/2026/03/WVGHOF_Noms_2026_Group-SQ.jpg)

March 5, 2026

The Strong’s World Video Game Hall of Fame announced the 12 finalists for induction:Angry Birds, Dragon Quest, The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, FIFA International Soccer, Frogger, Galaga, League of Legends, Mega Man, PaRappa the Rapper, RuneScape, Silent Hill, and Tokimeki Memorial.

[More Information](https://www.museumofplay.org/press-release/world-video-game-hall-of-fame-reveals-12-finalists-for-2026-induction/)

![Image 11: Atari Collection](https://www.museumofplay.org/app/uploads/2026/02/Pac-Man.jpg)

February 2, 2026

The Strong acquires a comprehensive collection of Atari materials about Atari’s home computer and console divisions from the early 1970s through the 2000s.

[More Information](https://www.museumofplay.org/press-release/the-strong-national-museum-of-play-acquires-atari-home-computer-and-console-division-collection/)

![Image 12: Arcade Online Exhibit](https://www.museumofplay.org/app/uploads/2025/11/Woman-playing-Starship-SQ.jpg)

November 10, 2025

The Strong launches an online exhibit in partnership with Google Arts & Culture, Insert Coin to Start: A History of Arcade Video Games in the 1970s.

[More Information](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/RgURNd2cWGbNPQ)

![Image 13: 2025 Toy Hall of Fame Inductees](https://www.museumofplay.org/app/uploads/2025/11/NTHOF_2025_Inductee-Group-SQ.jpg)

November 6, 2025

The Strong’s National Toy Hall of Fame inducts Battleship, Slime, and Trivial Pursuit.

[More Information](https://www.museumofplay.org/press-release/2025-toy-hall-of-fame-inductees-revealed/)

![Image 14: Dungeons & Dragons](https://www.museumofplay.org/app/uploads/2025/09/Advanced-DnD-SQ.jpg)

September 22, 2025

The Strong—in partnership with Google Arts & Culture—explores how Dungeons & Dragons has transformed play and culture by infusing the universal love of pretend into a game system set in a world of wizards and warriors, monsters, and treasure.

[More Information](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/jwUhqeUB49cvBg)

## Featured Online Exhibits

**Through its online exhibits, The Strong’s historians, curators, librarians, and archivists investigate the history, evolution, and cultural effects of play and playthings.**

These exhibits are also accessible through Google Arts & Culture, where The Strong is an official partner.

[View on Google Arts & Culture](https://artsandculture.google.com/partner/the-strong)

Online Exhibit

### Video Game History Timeline

Explore the history of video games, understand how the industry began and evolved, and discover the impact that electronic games have had on how people play, learn, and connect with each other in a free online timeline.

[Explore Timeline](https://www.museumofplay.org/video-game-history-timeline/)

Google Arts & Culture

### A Brief History of Black Doll Designers Since the 1950s

This online exhibit celebrates the role of Black designers in diversifying dolls to help children build pride and encourage conversation.

[View Exhibit](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/MAUx6pt9Wqp4Fg)

## Support and Affiliations

The Strong is an independent 501(c)(3) not-for-profit educational organization. It is funded in part by the Margaret Woodbury Strong Trust but also depends on private contributions from individuals, corporations, and foundations, and upon competitive grants from public agencies such as the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS) and the New York State Council on the Arts (NYSCA).

The Strong is accredited by the American Alliance of Museums and is an institutional member of AAM, the American Association for State and Local History (AASLH), the Association of Children’s Museums (ACM), and the Museum Association of New York (MANY).
